clinical/picu_core.title: PICU_Core
clinical/picu_core.content:
PICU and Pediatric Emergencies: Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in the PICU: weight based emergency doses without errors, safe standard concentration drips, sedation and withdrawal plans, and adult max doses as the ceiling.
Sources: AHA/AAP Pediatric Advanced Life Support guideline (2025, Part 8, Circulation 2025;152 suppl 2); Neurocritical Care Society and American Epilepsy Society status epilepticus guidelines (AES 2016; ESETT trial, NEJM 2019); ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines, DKA (2022); AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on maintenance IV fluids (2018); SCCM PANDEM guidelines for pediatric ICU pain, agitation, neuromuscular blockade, delirium and iatrogenic withdrawal (Pediatr Crit Care Med, 2022).

1. The pediatric rules

Dose in mg/kg, but never exceed the adult dose. A 70 kg teenager gets an adult dose.
Use the measured weight in kg. For obese children, know whether the drug uses actual or ideal weight.
Standard concentrations matched to the smart pump library; no custom concentrations unless required.
Check the volume can actually be measured (very small volumes need dilution).

2. PALS code doses (AHA 2025)




























































DrugDoseNotesEpinephrine (0.1 mg/mL)0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg), max 1 mg, every 3 to 5 minutes. ETT: 0.1 mg/kg2025: give as early as possible in nonshockable rhythmsAmiodarone5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus (max 300 mg), may repeat up to 15 mg/kg totalFor shock refractory VF or pulseless VTLidocaine1 mg/kg IV/IOAlternative to amiodaroneAdenosine0.1 mg/kg rapid push (max 6 mg); second dose 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg)SVT; rapid flush, closest portAtropine0.02 mg/kg IV (max single dose 0.5 mg)Bradycardia from vagal tone or AV blockCalcium chloride 10%20 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg) IV/IO, central preferredHyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, calcium channel blocker overdoseCalcium gluconate 10%60 mg/kg (0.6 mL/kg) IVPeripheral friendly option [VERIFY dose in St. Mary’s sheet]Dextrose0.5 to 1 g/kg (D10W 5 to 10 mL/kg)HypoglycemiaSodium bicarbonate1 mEq/kgNot routine; hyperkalemia or tricyclic overdoseDefibrillation2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, max 10 J/kg or adult doseNot a drug, but you’ll hear it
Quote it: “PALS 2025 emphasizes epinephrine as early as possible in nonshockable arrest; the dose is 0.01 mg/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL, max 1 mg.”
3. Status epilepticus






























TimeStepDose0 to 5 minStabilize, check glucoseDextrose if low5 to 20 minBenzodiazepineLorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg), may repeat once; or midazolam IM 10 mg (over 40 kg) or 5 mg (13 to 40 kg), single dose (AES 2016; updated 2026-10-23, was 0.2 mg/kg max 10 mg); or diazepam rectal20 to 40 minSecond line (ESETT: similar efficacy)Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg); or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1,500 mg PE); or valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3,000 mg)40+ minRefractoryInfusion (midazolam, pentobarbital, ketamine) with ICU and EEG
Pharmacist watch: fosphenytoin is dosed in PE (phenytoin equivalents); valproate is avoided in suspected mitochondrial or metabolic disease and in young children with unknown liver disease.
Status epilepticus timed ladder (AES 2016 and ESETT 2019)
flowchart TD
    Green["GREEN · 0 TO 20 MINUTES: CHECK GLUCOSE + FIRST LINE BENZODIAZEPINE<br/>0 to 5 min: Stabilize airway and breathing; check fingerstick glucose (give Dextrose D10W 5 to 10 mL/kg if low)<br/>5 to 20 min: Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg, may repeat once) OR Midazolam IM 10 mg (over 40 kg) or 5 mg (13 to 40 kg), single dose ✅"]
    Amber["AMBER · 20 TO 40 MINUTES: ESETT SECOND LINE (All 3 Equally Effective, Pick One Fast)<br/>Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg)<br/>OR Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1,500 mg PE)<br/>OR Valproate 40 mg/kg IV (max 3,000 mg; avoid in young children with unknown liver or mitochondrial disease) ✅✅"]

    Green --> Amber --> Red

    style Green fill:#166534,stroke:#16a34a,color:#ffffff
    style Amber fill:#92400e,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    style Red fill:#991b1b,stroke:#dc2626,color:#ffffff

Sources: American Epilepsy Society Status Epilepticus Guideline (2016); ESETT trial (NEJM 2019) ✅✅
Why benzodiazepines stop working if a seizure goes past 20 minutes (plain English):

The disappearing GABA doors: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, midazolam) stop seizures by locking onto GABA receptors (the brain’s natural calm down brakes). During the first 5 to 15 minutes of a seizure, those GABA receptors sit on the outside of brain cells where the drug can reach them. After 15 to 20 minutes of nonstop seizing, brain cells pull their GABA receptors inside the cell where benzodiazepines cannot reach them anymore, while excitatory receptors multiply on the surface. That is why giving a first benzodiazepine on time is critical, and why at 20 minutes you must switch to a second line drug (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate) that works through a completely different door ✅✅.

4. Pediatric DKA (ISPAD 2022)

Fluids first: 10 to 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus.
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h IV, no bolus, started after the first hour of fluids.
Potassium: if the child is hypokalemic, start potassium replacement before insulin (ISPAD 2022); many protocols hold insulin until K is at least 3.3 [VERIFY St. Mary’s cutoff]. If K is normal, add it with insulin; if high, wait for urine output. Adults are different: the 2024 adult consensus holds insulin until K is above 3.5 (see Insulin_IV_DKA).
Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 to 300 mg/dL (two bag system).
Cerebral edema (headache, falling heart rate, rising BP, change in mental status): mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 10 to 15 min, or 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg. Have it available.
Why pediatric DKA never gets an insulin bolus (plain English): A child’s brain is still growing inside a tight skull. If you push an IV insulin bolus or drop blood glucose too fast in the first hour, blood osmolality drops faster than brain cells can adjust, and water rushes into the child’s brain (cerebral edema, which can cause brain herniation). Giving isotonic fluids for the first hour and starting a gentle drip at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h with no bolus lets blood sugar come down smoothly (ISPAD 2022) ✅.

5. Rapid sequence intubation (pediatric)





























DrugDoseKetamine1 to 2 mg/kg IVEtomidate0.3 mg/kg IV (adrenal suppression; avoid in septic shock per many protocols)Rocuronium1 to 1.2 mg/kg IVSuccinylcholine2 mg/kg in infants, 1 to 1.5 mg/kg in children (avoid in hyperkalemia, neuromuscular disease, burns or crush after 24 to 48 h)Atropine premedicationNot routine; consider for infants or if bradycardia is likely
6. Sedation, analgesia and withdrawal

Common drips: fentanyl, morphine, midazolam, dexmedetomidine, ketamine.
After 5 or more days of opioid or benzodiazepine infusions, expect iatrogenic withdrawal. Units use a scoring tool (WAT-1) and a wean plan (for example enteral methadone or lorazepam). Pharmacists often write the wean.
Propofol: long, high dose infusions in children carry risk of propofol infusion syndrome.

7. Everyday pediatric dosing anchors

Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg every 6 hours (max 75 mg/kg/day, not over 4 g/day).
Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours (6 months and older; max 40 mg/kg/day).
Maintenance fluids: Holliday Segar 4/2/1 rule for rate; AAP 2018 recommends isotonic fluids with appropriate KCl and dextrose for most hospitalized children 28 days to 18 years.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg (max 8 mg per the Canadian Paediatric Society; weight bands 2, 4, 6 to 8 mg); age 6 months or older. Updated 2026-10-17 (was “max 4 mg in most protocols”); see Pediatric_Neonatal_Dosing.

8. Pediatric toxicology to know cold

Acetaminophen: NAC (21 hour IV protocol; know St. Mary’s regimen, many sites now use a two bag protocol).
Iron, tricyclics (bicarbonate), button battery (honey or sucralfate before arrival, per guidance), clonidine, sulfonylureas (octreotide).
Poison Control: 1 800 222 1222.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Pediatric code sheet or Broselow type system; who prepares drug doses at peds codes.
Standard pediatric drip concentrations in the pump library.
Status epilepticus order set (which second line agent).
DKA order set (two bag system?).
Sedation and withdrawal protocol (WAT-1, wean).

clinical/stroke_core.title: Stroke_Core
clinical/stroke_core.content:
Stroke (Comprehensive Stroke Center): Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in a stroke alert: confirm weight, check for contraindications (anticoagulants, recent surgery, platelets, glucose), prepare and double check the thrombolytic fast (door to needle goal), manage BP before and after, and set up antithrombotic therapy after.
Sources: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (Prabhakaran et al., Stroke, published January 26, 2026); AHA/ASA 2022 Guideline for Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage; AHA/ASA 2023 Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Guideline; FDA approval of tenecteplase (TNKase) for acute ischemic stroke (March 2025); Andexxa US market withdrawal (2025).

1. Ischemic stroke: thrombolysis (AHA/ASA 2026)

Tenecteplase is now equally preferred to alteplase (2026). Advantage: a single bolus, fewer mixing and infusion errors.
Time: within 4.5 hours of last known well. Selected patients up to 9 hours based on advanced imaging (2026).
Not for mild, nondisabling symptoms (symptoms that don’t affect daily activities or the ability to work).





















AgentDoseKey safety pointTenecteplase0.25 mg/kg IV bolus over 5 seconds, max 25 mgThe cardiac (STEMI) dose is different and higher. Use the stroke dose only; many sites stock a dedicated stroke kit or dosing chartAlteplase0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% as bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutesAfter the infusion, the dead volume in the tubing must be flushed so the full dose is given [VERIFY St. Mary’s procedure]
Before lytics: BP below 185/110. Glucose checked (treat if below 50; hypoglycemia can mimic stroke). Platelets and INR are not required before starting unless a problem is suspected, but know the contraindications (for example INR above 1.7, platelets below 100,000, therapeutic heparin or enoxaparin, or a recent DOAC dose) [VERIFY 2026 wording on DOACs].
After lytics, for 24 hours: BP below 180/105. No antithrombotics for 24 hours (unless specifically indicated). Neuro checks.
BP agents: labetalol 10 to 20 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes (may repeat once), nicardipine infusion 5 mg/h titrated by 2.5 mg/h every 5 to 15 minutes (max 15 mg/h), clevidipine 1 to 2 mg/h titrated (max 21 mg/h).
Angioedema after alteplase or tenecteplase (more common with ACE inhibitors): stop the infusion, give methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine and famotidine; epinephrine if it worsens; icatibant or C1 esterase inhibitor may be considered.
Bleeding after a thrombolytic: stop it; cryoprecipitate 10 units, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes or aminocaproic acid as an alternative [VERIFY order set].
Acute ischemic stroke thrombolysis and BP ladder
flowchart TD
    Step1["GREEN · READY FOR THROMBOLYSIS (Within 4.5 h of last known well)<br/>BP below 185/110 and glucose checked (not below 50)<br/>Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus over 5 seconds (max 25 mg)<br/>OR Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg): 10% over 1 min, 90% over 60 min ✅✅"]
    Step2["AMBER · FIRST 24 HOURS AFTER LYTICS (Protect Against Bleed)<br/>Keep BP below 180/105 for 24 hours<br/>Labetalol 10 to 20 mg IV over 1 to 2 min, or Nicardipine 5 mg/h titrated by 2.5 mg/h every 5 to 15 min (max 15 mg/h)<br/>NO aspirin, heparin, or other antithrombotics for 24 hours ✅✅"]
    Step3["RED · HARD STOPS AND EMERGENCY COMPLICATIONS<br/>DO NOT GIVE LYTICS if BP is 185/110 or higher, INR above 1.7, platelets below 100,000, or recent therapeutic anticoagulant<br/>BLEEDING AFTER LYTICS: Stop infusion; give Cryoprecipitate 10 units + Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min<br/>OROLINGUAL ANGIOEDEMA: Stop infusion; give Methylprednisolone + Diphenhydramine + Famotidine ✅"]

    Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3

    style Step1 fill:#166534,stroke:#16a34a,color:#ffffff
    style Step2 fill:#92400e,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    style Step3 fill:#991b1b,stroke:#dc2626,color:#ffffff

Sources: AHA/ASA 2026 Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline; FDA TNKase label (2025) ✅✅

How it works and timing in the body (plain English):

How tenecteplase and alteplase dissolve the clot: Both drugs turn plasminogen into plasmin, which acts like molecular scissors that cut up the fibrin mesh holding a blood clot together. Tenecteplase is a modified version of alteplase that stays in the blood longer (half life about 20 to 24 minutes vs 4 to 5 minutes for alteplase) and aims more specifically at fibrin inside the clot, which is why tenecteplase is a single 5 second IV push while alteplase requires a 1 minute bolus followed by a 60 minute infusion (AHA/ASA 2026) ✅✅.
Why BP must be below 185/110 before and below 180/105 after: Brain tissue starved of oxygen has fragile, leaky blood vessel walls. Pushing a clot busting drug while blood pressure is hammering against those fragile vessels above 185/110 can blow the vessel open and turn an ischemic stroke into a fatal brain bleed (hemorrhagic transformation) (AHA/ASA 2026) ✅.
Why stroke patients on ACE inhibitors get tongue swelling (angioedema) from lytics: Plasmin (activated by tenecteplase or alteplase) also turns on bradykinin, a chemical that makes lips and the tongue swell. Normally, ACE enzymes break down bradykinin; when a patient takes an ACE inhibitor (such as lisinopril), bradykinin cannot be broken down and builds up in the tongue and airway (AHA/ASA 2026) ✅.
Real shift picture (what happens when the stroke pager goes off): You hear “Stroke Alert, CT Scanner.” Before mixing anything, look at two numbers on the screen: the patient’s weight in kg and the blood pressure. If the vial in your hand is tenecteplase, remember the vial holds 50 mg (the heart attack size), while the maximum brain stroke dose is 25 mg (0.25 mg/kg). Draw up only the stroke dose into the syringe before handing it to the nurse so the extra 25 mg can never be pushed by mistake ✅.

2. Ischemic stroke: after the acute phase

Minor stroke or high risk TIA: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel, 21 days). 2026 update: can be used for NIHSS 4 or 5 (not only 3 or less) and can start within 72 hours.
Load clopidogrel 300 to 600 mg, then 75 mg daily; aspirin 160 to 325 mg load, then 81 mg daily.
Atrial fibrillation: start a DOAC; timing depends on stroke size (ELAN and TIMING trials support earlier starts) [VERIFY 2026 recommendation].
High intensity statin.
Glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL in the hospital.
VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin or heparin once safe; intermittent pneumatic compression.

3. Intracerebral hemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2022)

BP: for mild to moderate ICH with SBP 150 to 220, lowering to a target of 140 (keeping it in 130 to 150) is reasonable; avoid dropping below 130. Smooth, sustained control (nicardipine or clevidipine drips) matters.
Reversal (the pharmacist’s biggest job here):


































DrugReversalWarfarin4F-PCC (dose by INR and weight per protocol) + vitamin K 10 mg IVDabigatranIdarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials)Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban4F-PCC 50 units/kg (per protocol). Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in 2025Heparin infusionProtamine 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2 to 3 hours (max 50 mg)EnoxaparinProtamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if within 8 hours (0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8 to 12 hours)AntiplateletsPlatelet transfusion is not recommended unless the patient is going to surgery (PATCH trial)
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) anticoagulant reversal ladder
flowchart TD
    Green["GREEN · TARGETED SPECIFIC REVERSAL (Fast Direct Lock)<br/>Dabigatran: Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials)<br/>Warfarin: 4F-PCC (25 to 50 units/kg by INR and weight) + Vitamin K 10 mg IV ✅✅"]
    Amber["AMBER · FACTOR REPLETION OR PARTIAL REVERSAL<br/>Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Edoxaban: 4F-PCC 50 units/kg IV per protocol<br/>Heparin infusion: Protamine 1 mg per 100 units given in last 2 to 3 hours (max 50 mg)<br/>Enoxaparin: Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if within 8 hours (0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8 to 12 hours) ✅✅"]
    Red["RED · DO NOT DO IN ICH<br/>NO Platelet transfusion for antiplatelet bleeds unless going to neurosurgery (PATCH trial)<br/>NO Andexanet alfa (withdrawn from US market in 2025)<br/>DO NOT drop SBP below 130 mmHg (target 140, range 130 to 150) ✅✅"]

    Green --> Amber --> Red

    style Green fill:#166534,stroke:#16a34a,color:#ffffff
    style Amber fill:#92400e,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    style Red fill:#991b1b,stroke:#dc2626,color:#ffffff

Sources: AHA/ASA 2022 Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage Guideline; PATCH trial (Lancet 2016) ✅✅

No seizure prophylaxis routinely. Treat hyperglycemia and fever. VTE prophylaxis with heparin or enoxaparin can start 24 to 48 hours after the bleed is stable.

4. Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2023)

Nimodipine 60 mg orally or by tube every 4 hours for 21 days. Oral only; never IV (deaths have occurred when capsule contents were injected; FDA boxed warning). If BP drops, 30 mg every 2 hours.
BP control before the aneurysm is secured (common target SBP below 160) [VERIFY].
Reversal of any anticoagulant; levetiracetam is preferred over phenytoin if an antiseizure drug is used.

How nimodipine works and why it can NEVER be given IV (plain English):

Why we give nimodipine for 21 days after a burst brain aneurysm: Between days 3 and 21 after blood spills around the outside of the brain, irritated cerebral arteries clamp down in delayed spasm (cerebral vasospasm), which can cause a secondary stroke. Nimodipine is a fat soluble calcium channel blocker that enters the brain and keeps those vessels open (AHA/ASA 2023) ✅.
Why injecting nimodipine IV is fatal: Nimodipine comes as a liquid filled gel capsule so nurses can extract the liquid for patients with a feeding tube. Because it is drawn up into a syringe, nurses have accidentally connected that syringe to an IV line. Swallowed in the gut, the liver clears most of the drug smoothly over time; injected straight into a vein, the concentrated liquid and its alcohol solvent cause instant, irreversible cardiovascular collapse and death. Always use oral/enteral only syringes labeled “Not for IV Use” (FDA boxed warning; ISMP) ✅✅.

5. Stroke alert checklist (pharmacist)

Weight: measured or estimated? (Tenecteplase dosing is weight banded.)
Last known well time. Anticoagulant, and when was the last dose?
BP below 185/110? If not, have labetalol or nicardipine ready.
Glucose done?
Prepare tenecteplase or alteplase; independent double check of dose and drug (tenecteplase vs alteplase look alike packaging; stroke vs cardiac dose).
Document time of bolus (door to needle).

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Which thrombolytic St. Mary’s uses for stroke, and the dosing chart.
Stroke alert pharmacist response (does pharmacy go to the ED or CT?).
Anticoagulant reversal order set (4F-PCC dosing method).
Post thrombectomy BP targets in the order set.

clinical/trauma_core.title: Trauma_Core
clinical/trauma_core.content:
Trauma (Level I): Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in a trauma activation: TXA on time, anticoagulant reversal fast, RSI drugs, antibiotics for open fractures, tetanus, brain injury osmotherapy, and later pain, VTE prophylaxis and withdrawal.
Sources: CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010) and CRASH-3 (Lancet 2019, TBI); ACS TQIP best practice guidelines (massive transfusion; TBI); Brain Trauma Foundation 4th ed. (2016); EAST practice management guidelines (open fracture antibiotics; VTE prophylaxis); CDC tetanus guidance; AHA/ASA 2022 ICH reversal table (Stroke_Core).

1. Tranexamic acid (TXA)

Dose (CRASH-2): 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
Timing: within 3 hours of injury. Benefit is greatest when given early; after 3 hours it may cause harm (CRASH-2 subgroup).
TBI: CRASH-3 showed benefit in mild to moderate TBI when given within 3 hours.
Some EMS systems give 2 g as a single prehospital bolus; check what was already given before ordering more.

Quote it: “CRASH-2: 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, and only within 3 hours of injury.”
2. Massive transfusion

Balanced ratio of plasma, platelets and red cells, close to 1:1:1 (PROPPR trial, ACS TQIP).
Calcium: citrate in blood products drops ionized calcium. Expect calcium chloride 1 g IV (central preferred) or calcium gluconate 3 g per protocol, guided by ionized calcium.
Watch potassium (rises with stored blood) and temperature.

Trauma bay first hour drug and safety ladder
flowchart TD
    Green["GREEN · GIVE EARLY (Within 1 to 3 Hours of Injury)<br/>TXA: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 hours (ONLY within 3 hours of injury; check EMS doses) ✅<br/>Open fractures: Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more) within 1 hour; add gram negative coverage for Type III ✅<br/>Massive transfusion: Give Calcium chloride 1 g IV (central) or Calcium gluconate 3 g IV to replace calcium bound by blood bag citrate ✅"]
    Amber["AMBER · RAPID SEQUENCE INTUBATION (Match to Blood Pressure and Timing)<br/>Shock or hypotension: Ketamine 1 to 2 mg/kg IV or Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV (avoid full dose propofol in shock) ✅<br/>Paralytic: Rocuronium 1 to 1.2 mg/kg IV (lasts 45 to 60 min; start fentanyl and sedation immediately after tube placement) ✅"]
    Red["RED · TRAUMA BAY HARD STOPS<br/>NO TXA if more than 3 hours after injury (increased bleeding mortality in CRASH-2) ✅<br/>NO Succinylcholine in hyperkalemia, or 24 to 48 hours after burns, crush, or spinal cord injury ✅<br/>NO steroids in TBI (increased death in CRASH trial); 23.4% saline is CENTRAL LINE ONLY ✅"]

    Green --> Amber --> Red

    style Green fill:#166534,stroke:#16a34a,color:#ffffff
    style Amber fill:#92400e,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    style Red fill:#991b1b,stroke:#dc2626,color:#ffffff

Sources: CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010); ACS TQIP Massive Transfusion & TBI Guidelines; Brain Trauma Foundation 4th ed. (2016); EAST Open Fracture Guideline (2022) ✅✅
How trauma drugs work in the body (plain English for fast recall):

Why bags of blood drop the patient’s calcium (the citrate sponge): Blood bank bags contain citrate to keep donated blood from clotting in the bag, and citrate works by grabbing onto calcium. When a trauma patient gets rapid units of blood and plasma, all that citrate enters the patient’s veins and sponges up the patient’s own ionized calcium. Without calcium, the heart cannot squeeze (hypotension) and blood cannot clot (coagulopathy). Giving calcium chloride 1 g IV (central) or calcium gluconate 3 g IV refills the calcium tank (ACS TQIP) ✅.
Why succinylcholine is safe in the first hour of a burn/crush, but fatal 24 to 48 hours later: Succinylcholine paralyzes muscles by opening acetylcholine channels on muscle cells, which lets a tiny puff of potassium leak out (normally raising K by about 0.5 mEq/L). Starting 24 to 48 hours after a major burn, crush injury, or spinal cord injury, damaged muscle cells sprout thousands of extra receptors across their entire surface. If you give succinylcholine then, all those extra doors fly open at once and dump a massive wave of potassium into the blood, stopping the heart ✅.
Why paralyzed patients wake up terrified if you forget post intubation analgesia/sedation: Etomidate (induction) wears off in 5 to 10 minutes, while rocuronium (paralytic) keeps the patient completely unable to move or blink for 45 to 60 minutes. Always hang fentanyl and propofol or dexmedetomidine immediately after the breathing tube goes in ✅.

3. Anticoagulated trauma patient
Same reversal table as ICH (Stroke_Core section 3). Find out the anticoagulant and the time of the last dose immediately; this is where pharmacists save minutes.
4. Rapid sequence intubation (adult)



































DrugDoseWatchKetamine1 to 2 mg/kg IVGood in hypotension; raises secretionsEtomidate0.3 mg/kg IVAdrenal suppression (single dose)Propofol1 to 2.5 mg/kg IVHypotension: avoid or reduce in shockRocuronium1 to 1.2 mg/kg IVReversal: sugammadex 16 mg/kg for immediate reversalSuccinylcholine1 to 1.5 mg/kg IVAvoid with hyperkalemia, burns or crush injury after 24 to 48 hours, spinal cord injury after the first days, neuromuscular disease, history of malignant hyperthermia
Post intubation: analgesia first (fentanyl), then sedation (propofol, dexmedetomidine). Paralyzed patients must be sedated; rocuronium lasts longer than etomidate.
5. Traumatic brain injury (BTF 2016; ACS TQIP)

Avoid hypotension and hypoxia.
Osmotherapy: mannitol 0.25 to 1 g/kg IV, or hypertonic saline (3% 250 mL, or 23.4% 30 mL central line only, ISMP high alert).
Seizure prophylaxis for severe TBI for 7 days (phenytoin per BTF; levetiracetam is widely used) [VERIFY St. Mary’s choice].
Steroids are not recommended in TBI (CRASH trial).

6. Open fractures (EAST 2022)

Start antibiotics as soon as possible (within 1 hour).
Type I and II: cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more).
Type III: cefazolin plus gram negative coverage (for example ceftriaxone, or cefazolin + gentamicin per protocol) [VERIFY order set]. Add penicillin for farm or soil contamination.

7. Tetanus (CDC)

Clean minor wound: Tdap or Td if more than 10 years since last dose.
Dirty or major wound: Tdap or Td if more than 5 years; plus tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM if vaccination history is unknown or fewer than 3 doses.

8. After the trauma bay

VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin (commonly 30 mg every 12 hours or 40 mg daily, weight and anti Xa adjusted per protocol) once bleeding risk allows, often within 24 to 48 hours (EAST, ACS TQIP) [VERIFY protocol].
Pain: multimodal (acetaminophen, NSAIDs if no bleeding or kidney concern, regional anesthesia, ketamine, opioids). Rib fractures benefit from regional blocks and scheduled nonopioids.
Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA based benzodiazepines or phenobarbital protocols; thiamine before glucose.
Stress ulcer prophylaxis for coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease (SCCM/ASHP 2024; ventilation alone is not an established indication). Updated 2026-10-17 (was “ventilated or coagulopathic”); see Adult_Critical_Care.
Burns: Parkland formula, 4 mL/kg per % TBSA of lactated Ringer’s in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours (from time of burn).
Spinal cord injury: high dose methylprednisolone is not recommended routinely.

Trauma activation checklist (pharmacist)

Weight (estimated) and allergies.
Anticoagulants or antiplatelets? Last dose time?
TXA: injury time? Under 3 hours? Already given by EMS?
RSI kit ready; post intubation sedation.
Open fracture: cefazolin. Tetanus status.
Head injury: hypertonic saline or mannitol ready.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Trauma activation pharmacist response.
TXA protocol and EMS doses.
Massive transfusion protocol and calcium replacement.
Open fracture antibiotic order set; VTE prophylaxis protocol for trauma.

curriculum/12_week_plan.title: 12_Week_Plan
curriculum/12_week_plan.content:
12 Week Plan (PGY1 equivalent, self directed)
Built on the ASHP PGY1 competency areas: R1 Patient Care, R2 Practice Advancement, R3 Leadership, R4 Teaching and Education. Each week: 1 module page, 5 daily cases, 1 “quote it” drill, 1 safety alert.
Order is set by risk at St. Mary’s: the specialty areas (NICU, PICU, L&D) and the areas where a PRN pharmacist is alone at night (codes, trauma, stroke, anticoagulation) come first.



















































































WeekModuleWhy nowStatus1LD_Obstetrics_CorePriority area; high alert drugs (magnesium, oxytocin)Built2NICU_CorePriority area; 10 fold error riskBuilt3PICU_CorePriority area; weight based emergenciesBuilt4Codes_Resuscitation (ACLS 2025, PALS 2025, NRP 2025)You may be the only pharmacist at a codeBuilt5Stroke_Core: thrombolysis, BP, reversal, ICHComprehensive stroke centerBuilt6Trauma_Core: TXA, massive transfusion, anticoagulant reversal, RSI, pain and sedationLevel I traumaBuilt7Anticoagulation: heparin, enoxaparin, DOACs, warfarin, HITMost common high alert verificationsBuilt8Infectious Diseases and Stewardship: sepsis, vancomycin AUC, aminoglycosides, beta lactam allergyDaily volumeBuilt9Adult Critical Care: vasopressors, sedation (PADIS), DKA, electrolytesOvernight ICU callsBuilt10IV Room and Sterile Compounding (USP 797, 800), pediatric and neonatal TPNBig at St. Mary’sBuilt11Medication Safety and Regulatory: ISMP high alert list, Joint Commission NPSGs, Florida lawWhat leadership is judged onBuilt12Practice_Advancement: pick and start one projectWhat makes you look like a residentBuilt
Residency style deliverables (do these and leadership notices)

One medication use evaluation (MUE) or quality project in your first 6 months. Examples: time to TXA in trauma activations, magnesium monitoring compliance on L&D, IV to PO opportunities, vancomycin AUC target attainment. Ask your manager which one helps the department.
One inservice to nurses or pharmacy staff (15 minutes). Example: “Magnesium sulfate toxicity: what the nurse sees first.”
An intervention log. Count and categorize what you catch (dose, duplication, interaction, renal adjustment, allergy). This is the number that proves your value.
Board certification path (later): BCPS is the standard credential that signals residency level knowledge. Florida does not require it; it is optional and a long term goal.

Continuing education priorities

ASHP Midyear (December) and ASHP Summer Meetings; FSHP (Florida Society of Health System Pharmacists) annual meeting.
Florida license renewal CE, including the required medication error and controlled substance hours (her first renewal by September 30, 2027: 15 hours, see Med_Safety_and_Florida_Law) ✅ Florida Board of Pharmacy: renewal.
PALS and ACLS provider courses are worth taking even if not required for your role. They give you the code language the teams use.

curriculum/daily_routine.title: Daily_Routine
curriculum/daily_routine.content:
Daily and Shift Routine
The pharmacist workup (use for every order you verify that is not routine)
Based on the JCPP Pharmacists’ Patient Care Process: Collect, Assess, Plan, Implement, Follow up.

Who: age, weight (dosing weight for peds and neonates, in kg only), height, allergies with reaction type, pregnancy or lactation status.
Why: indication. If you can’t name it, ask.
Organs: SCr and CrCl or eGFR, urine output, LFTs, platelets and INR for anticoagulants.
Drug check: dose, route, frequency, duration, max dose, concentration, compatibility, duplication, interactions, high alert status.
Monitor: what level, lab or vital sign tells you it is working or hurting, and when.
Communicate: if you call, use SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. End with a specific recommendation and a guideline you can name.

How to sound like a resident on the phone

“Dr. ___, this is Shallanda, the pharmacist. I’m calling about [patient] in [room]. The [drug] order is [dose]; with a CrCl of 28, the [source, year] recommends [change]. Would you like me to adjust it to [specific order]?”

Name the source and year. Give the exact order. Let them say yes.
Daily 20 minutes

1 case from Cases_LD_NICU_PICU, timed, out loud.
1 item from ISMP or FDA (see Stay_Current).

Weekly 2 hours

1 module page, then the “Verify locally” list for that module at work.


Night Shift Phone Call & Pager Survival Guide
When you are the only pharmacist covering a unit or working evenings and nights, the phone and pager can feel intimidating at first. Use this decision ladder to triage what happens first, and use the scripts below so you never freeze on the phone.
flowchart TD
    CALL["Incoming Call or Pager Alert"] --> STAT["1. STAT Bedside Emergency:<br/>Code Blue, PALS, NRP, Stroke Alert, Trauma Alert, Massive PPH, Anaphylaxis, Extravasation"]
    CALL --> URG["2. Urgent Drip or Lab Call:<br/>DKA potassium drop, Heparin aPTT supra-therapeutic, Pressor line question, Missing STAT antibiotic in sepsis"]
    CALL --> ROUT["3. Routine Floor Call:<br/>IV Y-site check, Crushing meds for NG tube, Missing routine Pyxis dose, IV to PO switch"]

    STAT --> ACT1["Drop routine queue immediately.<br/>Check weight and allergies, grab emergency kit or verify STAT order within minutes.<br/>(ACLS/PALS 2025, AHA/ASA Stroke 2026, SSC 2021)"]
    URG --> ACT2["Open patient chart in PowerChart + Hospital Protocol.<br/>Verify lab trend, hold or adjust per protocol, and give the nurse exact instructions.<br/>(ISMP High Alert 2024)"]
    ROUT --> ACT3["Open Trissel's, Lexicomp Administration, or MAR.<br/>Give a clear Yes or No with the reason, and document if clinical.<br/>(ASHP Drug Information Guidelines)"]

    style CALL fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,color:#0f172a,stroke-width:2px
    style STAT fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#991b1b,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px
    style URG fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#92400e,color:#78350f,stroke-width:2px
    style ROUT fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#166534,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px
    style ACT1 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#991b1b,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px
    style ACT2 fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#92400e,color:#78350f,stroke-width:2px
    style ACT3 fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#166534,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px

Sources: JCPP Pharmacists’ Patient Care Process; ISMP High Alert Medications 2024; AHA/ASA 2026; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021.
Word for word scripts for the 7 most common hospital calls













































Who is calling & what happenedWhat you check first (10 seconds)Exact words to say on the phone1. Nurse: “Can I Y-site Drug A and Drug B together?”Open Trissel’s IV Compatibility (Y-site tab). Check the exact concentrations and diluents on the patient’s MAR (see IV_Compatibility).• If Compatible: “Yes, according to Trissel’s, [Drug A] at [conc] and [Drug B] at [conc] are Y-site compatible.”• If Incompatible or Variable/No Data: “No, do not Y-site those two; they can precipitate or inactivate each other. Please run them in separate lumens, or pause one, flush the line with normal saline before and after, and then run the second.”2. Nurse: “My DKA patient’s potassium just came back at 3.1 and the insulin drip is running!”Open PowerChart Labs: check K+, SCr, urine output, and Mg (see Insulin_IV_DKA).”Hold the insulin drip right now. Because insulin pushes potassium into the cells, running insulin with a potassium below 3.5 mEq/L can trigger a fatal arrhythmia (ADA/EASD hyperglycemic crises consensus 2024). Let’s start IV potassium repletion per protocol (max 10 mEq/h peripherally) and check magnesium; once repeat potassium is 3.5 mEq/L or higher, we can restart the insulin drip.”3. Nurse: “The norepinephrine IV infiltrated and the patient’s arm looks pale and cold!”Open IV_Compatibility and Norepinephrine. Locate phentolamine right away.”Stop the norepinephrine on that line, aspirate what you can from the catheter, then remove it, and restart the pressor on a different line immediately. Do not put a cold pack on it; elevate the arm and use a warm compress. We are sending phentolamine 5 to 10 mg diluted in 10 to 15 mL normal saline for local subcutaneous infiltration around the site as soon as possible (works best within 12 hours per FDA label).“4. Nurse: “Can I crush the patient’s home meds for their new NG tube?”Check every oral order against the ISMP Do Not Crush list and Lexicomp Administration tab (see Med_Safety_and_Florida_Law).”Never crush extended release, enteric coated, or sublingual tablets. Let me check their MAR right now: I will switch any extended release or enteric coated meds to an immediate release tablet or oral liquid equivalent and re-time any levothyroxine, phenytoin, or fluoroquinolone around tube feeds.”5. Nurse: “The patient has a penicillin allergy and the doctor ordered cefepime (or ceftriaxone)!”Check allergy reaction type on the banner + side chain similarity (see ID_Core).• If rash/hives or unknown (non severe): “Cefepime and ceftriaxone have completely different R1 side chains from penicillins, so cross reactivity is below 1 to 2% (AAAAI/ACAAI 2022). It can be given without skin testing (AAAAI/ACAAI 2022).”• If SJS, TEN, or DRESS: “Because the patient had a severe blistering reaction (SJS/TEN/DRESS), we must avoid all beta lactams; I am calling the physician right now to switch to a non beta lactam.”6. Stroke Alert or Trauma Alert Pager Goes OffOpen Stroke_Core or Trauma_Core and pull up the patient’s weight, last known well time, INR/platelets, and anticoagulant history.• Stroke: “I have the patient’s weight of [X] kg. If we give tenecteplase, the stroke dose is 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) IV push over 5 seconds; blood pressure must be below 185/110 before we push (AHA/ASA 2026).”• Trauma: “If we are within 3 hours of injury with significant bleeding, TXA is 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over 8 hours (CRASH-2 2010), and we have calcium gluconate ready for massive transfusion.”7. Physician pushes back: “Just verify it anyway, that’s how I always order it.”Stay calm, cite the exact safety mechanism and hospital policy or FDA boxed warning, and offer the safe alternative that accomplishes their goal.”Dr. ___, I want to get this started for your patient right away. The reason I cannot verify [current order] as written is [specific safety risk, for example: CrCl is 22 mL/min, which raises enoxaparin levels and bleeding risk, and the FDA label calls for once daily dosing below 30 mL/min]. I can modify it right now to [safe protocol dose] so the nurse can give it immediately. Does that work for you?” (If a life threatening error still cannot be resolved, escalate up your pharmacy clinical leadership chain per hospital policy.)

curriculum/practice_advancement.title: Practice_Advancement
curriculum/practice_advancement.content:
Practice Advancement (Module 12)
Why it matters: a residency trained pharmacist is expected to improve the system, not only work in it. One small, finished project in your first 6 months does more for how leaders see you than any credential.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]

1. The pick: magnesium sulfate infusion safety on L&D (MUE)
Recommendation: start here. It sits in a priority area, magnesium is an ISMP high alert drug, the criteria come straight from the FDA label and ACOG (Magnesium_Sulfate, LD_Obstetrics_Core), the patient numbers are small enough to review by hand, and it measures process (a quality project for St. Mary’s, not research).
Backup picks (same method, if leadership prefers another area):



































ProjectPriority areaWhat you measureSource pageTime to TXA in trauma activationsTraumaPercent given within 3 h of injury; second gram startedTrauma_Core, JC_CRASH-2Thrombolytic dose accuracyStrokeTenecteplase stroke dose used (not the cardiac dose); vial waste done for alteplaseThrombolytics_StrokeDOAC dosing at admissionAnticoagulationPercent of apixaban and rivaroxaban doses matching label criteriaAnticoagulation_CoreVancomycin stop at 48 h with negative MRSA naresIDDays of therapy savedID_Core
Before anything: ask your manager which project helps the department, and use only St. Mary’s systems for patient data. Nothing with patient identifiers leaves the hospital, and none of it goes into this wiki.
2. Draft criteria for the magnesium MUE





















































#CriterionTargetSource1Indication documented (severe preeclampsia, eclampsia, or fetal neuroprotection)100%LD_Obstetrics_Core2Loading dose 4 to 6 g over 15 to 20 min, maintenance 1 to 2 g/h100%Magnesium_Sulfate3Renal adjustment when SCr is elevated or urine output is low (label: 4 g load, 1 g/h, max 20 g per 48 h)100% of eligibleMagnesium_Sulfate4Premixed bag and dedicated pump channel used100%ISMP (Med_Safety_and_Florida_Law)5Reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output documented on schedule90% or more ⚠️ set with nursing6Calcium gluconate available and ordered as needed100%Magnesium_Sulfate7Stopped about 24 h after delivery or last seizure90% or moreLD_Obstetrics_Core
Thresholds are drafts; set them with the L&D team. ⚠️ [VERIFY against St. Mary’s order set]
3. The method (ASHP MUE guideline, 2021, FOCUS PDCA)

Find the need (high alert drug, past events, new guideline).
Organize the team (pharmacy, L&D nursing, an obstetrician) and get approval.
Clarify criteria, objectives, timeline, data collection and how results are shared.
Understand causes when results miss targets.
Select the fix, favoring hard wired changes (order set, pump library) over reminders.
Plan, 7. Do, 8. Check with follow up data, 9. Act to sustain and share.
✅ [1]

Which drugs make good MUE targets: high risk or high alert, high cost, high volume, a new safety alert, or not matching the formulary or guidelines ✅ [1].
Improvement cycles: the IHI Model for Improvement starts with “What are we trying to accomplish?”, then tests changes in small Plan Do Study Act cycles ✅ [2].
4. Quality improvement or research?

Research = systematic work meant to produce generalizable knowledge, involving human subjects (interaction or identifiable private information). It needs IRB review before it starts ✅ [3].
QI for your own hospital usually doesn’t need IRB approval, but if you might publish or present it, ask the IRB for a determination first ✅ [3].
Rule of thumb: ask St. Mary’s IRB before collecting any data if a poster is the goal ⚠️ [VERIFY Tenet IRB process].

5. Timeline (PRN friendly)





























MonthStep1 to 2Learn the workflow; start the intervention log; pitch the project to your manager3Final criteria; IRB determination if presenting; data collection form4Collect baseline data (20 to 30 patients is typical for a single site MUE ⚠️)5Analyze; present to pharmacy and L&D; propose one fix6Re check after the fix; write a one page summary; submit a poster abstract
Where to present: FSHP annual meeting or ASHP Midyear (abstract deadlines are months ahead; Midyear posters are usually due in the fall) ⚠️ [VERIFY dates on ashp.org and fshp.org].
6. The other two deliverables

Intervention log: count what you catch, by category. Use the tool in My Tools (no patient identifiers). The monthly total is your value in numbers.
One 15 minute inservice: “Magnesium sulfate toxicity: what the nurse sees first” pairs with this project. Outline: why it matters (high alert), reflexes before breathing, the numbers (label levels), the antidote, one case, 3 questions.

Sources

Afanasjeva J, et al. ASHP guidelines on medication use evaluation. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2021;78:168-175 · summary: ASHP Guidelines on Medication Use Evaluation (AJHP 2021)

UConn Health HSPP: Quality assurance, quality improvement and research

Antimicrobial Guide (empiric regimens by infection, adults)
Her own quick guide, built from public guideline summaries. Normal kidney function doses; adjust for CrCl. Always check St. Mary’s antibiogram and order sets first, and narrow once cultures return.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Background: ID_Core

Pneumonia

The Golden Rule of Hospital Pharmacy: Hospital Protocol Beats the Textbook
Before you quote Lexicomp or UpToDate to a physician or nurse, always check St. Mary’s Cerner Order Set, Hospital Policy, or Smart Pump Library first (see Stay_Current).

Side by side guide: Trissel’s vs Lexicomp vs NeoFax vs Sanford vs Briggs








































ResourceWhen to open it firstWhat trap to watch out for (Plain English)Trissel’s IV Compatibility (accessed via the IV Compatibility tab in Lexicomp or Micromedex)Nurse asks: “Can I Y-site vancomycin with piperacillin tazobactam?” or “How long is this diluted bag stable?”Check the right tab and concentration:• Y-Site tab: Two separate bags meeting at the tubing port near the patient (only mixes for a few minutes in the line).• Admixture (Solution) tab: Mixed together inside the same IV bag for hours.• Concentration matters: Ampicillin is stable much longer in NS than D5W, and high concentrations precipitate faster. Vancomycin and beta lactams can precipitate at certain concentrations.• “Variable” or “No Data”: Click into the study details. If your patient’s concentration is higher than the tested concentration, or if there is no data, treat as Incompatible and flush the line with NS between drugs or use a separate lumen (see IV_Compatibility).Lexicomp (Adult) vs MicromedexEvery routine adult verification: renal CrCl adjustments, hepatic adjustments, black box warnings, max daily doses, administration rates, and drug interactions.How to use them together:• Lexicomp is fastest at the bench for clean dosing by indication, CrCl cutoffs, and administration rate (push vs piggyback).• Micromedex is your tie breaker when Lexicomp is vague, when you need deeper toxicology (Poisindex), or when checking detailed Trissel’s solution stability tables.NeoFax vs Lexi-Peds (Taketomo Pediatric Handbook)NeoFax: Any baby in the NICU or under 28 days old.Lexi-Peds: Infants over 28 days, children, and adolescents in PICU or general pediatrics.Never use Adult Lexicomp for a baby:• Premature babies clear drugs slowly because their kidneys and liver are still developing.• NeoFax doses by Gestational Age (GA) or Postmenstrual Age (PMA = GA + weeks since birth) plus Postnatal Age (PNA = days since birth) (for example, NICU gentamicin every 24, 36, or 48 hours; see NICU_Core).• Lexi-Peds gives weight based mg/kg dosing and the adult ceiling cap (never exceed the adult dose in a heavy teenager; see Pediatric_Neonatal_Dosing).St. Mary’s Antibiogram + Sanford GuideDoctor asks: “What empiric antibiotic should we start for this ICU pneumonia or urosepsis?” or “Does oral step down work here?”Local resistance beats national averages:• Sanford Guide tells you which bugs a drug covers in general and gives clean renal antibiotic dosing tables.• St. Mary’s Antibiogram tells you what percentage of local Pseudomonas, E. coli, or MRSA at St. Mary’s is actually susceptible this year (see ID_Core and Antimicrobial_Guide).Briggs (Pregnancy) & LactMed (Breastfeeding)OB nurse or physician asks: “Can this mom take labetalol, enoxaparin, or sertraline while pregnant or breastfeeding?”Letters A, B, C, D, X are gone:• The FDA replaced pregnancy letter categories with the PLLR narrative (Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations, Data). Use Briggs or the FDA label PLLR section for pregnancy.• For breastfeeding, open LactMed (NIH, free) and check the Relative Infant Dose (RID): an RID below 10% is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding for full term infants (see Pregnancy_Lactation).CredibleMeds + ISMP ListsChecking QT prolongation stacking (ondansetron + haloperidol + azithromycin + methadone) or whether a pill can be crushed for an NG/OG tube.• CredibleMeds separates drugs that clearly cause Torsades de Pointes (“Known Risk”) from drugs that only prolong QTc under certain conditions (check K above 4.0 and Mg above 2.0).• ISMP Do Not Crush (and Lexicomp’s Administration section) stops you from crushing extended release (ER/XR), enteric coated (EC), or hazardous tablets (see Med_Safety_and_Florida_Law).

Pediatric and Neonatal Dosing
Her own quick reference for the floor, ED and NICU questions that come at night. Emergency and code doses live on PICU_Core (PALS 2025, status epilepticus, RSI) and NICU_Core (NRP, caffeine, dextrose). For anything not here, use St. Mary’s pediatric reference (pediatric dosage handbook or Neofax through St. Mary’s) and the order sets.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]

1. The 6 checks on every pediatric order

Weight in kg, measured, current, and the same weight everywhere (pounds entered as kg is the classic 2.2 fold error).
mg/kg dose and interval for this indication.
Never above the adult max (per dose and per day). Once a child reaches about adult weight, adult dosing applies.
Concentration and volume make sense for the syringe or pump (decimal errors are 10 fold errors).
Age limits: neonates (first 28 days) and preterm infants dose by gestational and postnatal age.
Duplicates: acetaminophen hides in combination products.

drug-hub/pregnancy_lactation.content:
Pregnancy and Lactation
Her own quick reference for L&D, postpartum and NICU mothers. LactMed is the primary free source for breastfeeding (LactMed, NIH); the AAP calls it the most complete and current resource ✅ [1]. For pregnancy, read the label’s section 8.1 on DailyMed; Briggs is available through St. Mary’s.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]

1. How to answer “Is it safe?”

Pregnancy: the old A, B, C, D, X letters were removed by the FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (effective June 30, 2015). Labels now have 8.1 Pregnancy (risk summary, clinical considerations, data, registry), 8.2 Lactation, and 8.3 Females and Males of Reproductive Potential ✅✅ [2][3]. Don’t answer with a letter.
Lactation: look up the drug in LactMed. Use the relative infant dose (RID): the infant’s dose from milk as a percent of the mother’s weight adjusted dose. Under 10% is generally acceptable ✅ [1].
Better choices in breastfeeding: short half life, high protein binding, low oral bioavailability, large molecule, RID under 10% ✅ [1].
Consider the infant: preterm and newborns clear drugs slowly.
Give a clear answer and a plan (“compatible; watch the baby for sleepiness”), not “consult your doctor.”

2. Quick answers for L&D and postpartum














































































































Drug or classPregnancyBreastfeedingCheckSourcesNSAIDs (ibuprofen, ketorolac)Avoid from 20 weeks (fetal kidney injury, low amniotic fluid); if needed 20 to 30 weeks, lowest dose, shortest time, ultrasound if more than 48 h; avoid from 30 weeks (ductus closure). Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Boxed warning: arterial and venous thromboembolic events. Not studied in patients with a thromboembolic event in the prior 3 months ✅ [1].
Warfarin reversal (labeled use), with vitamin K

































Pre treatment INRDose (units of factor IX per kg)MaxCheckSources2 to below 425 units/kg2,500 units✅✅[1] label; [2] Children’s Mercy guideline4 to 635 units/kg3,500 units✅✅[1][2]above 650 units/kg5,000 units✅✅[1][2]

Dose by weight up to 100 kg; don’t exceed the max above 100 kg ✅ [1].
Give vitamin K at the same time (4F-PCC wears off before warfarin does) ✅✅ [1][2]. Adult major bleeding: vitamin K 10 mg IV ✅ (AHA/ASA ICH 2022, see Stroke_Core).
Infusion: 0.12 mL/kg/min (about 3 units/kg/min), max 8.4 mL/min ✅ [1].
Repeat dosing is not recommended by the label ✅ [1].
Check INR about 30 minutes after the infusion ✅ [2].

Factor Xa inhibitor bleeding (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban), off label

Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Warfarin starves the liver so it cannot finish making the 4 vitamin K dependent clotting factors (Factors II, VII, IX, and X: think “1972”). Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) requires thawing and pouring liters of fluid into the patient. 4F-PCC (Kcentra) is “instant concentrated clotting factors in a small vial”: it hands the patient ready made Factors II, VII, IX, and X (plus Proteins C and S) in minutes.Dosing is always written in units of Factor IX per kg, and dosing weight is capped at 100 kg ✅ [1][2].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• 4F-PCC onset: Drops the INR below 1.4 within 30 minutes of finishing the infusion ✅ [1][2].• Why it wears off: Factor VII inside the 4F-PCC vial has a half life of only 4 to 6 hours, whereas warfarin lasts 2 to 5 days.• Vitamin K IV onset: Takes 4 to 6 hours for the liver to start building its own fresh clotting factors, and 12 to 24 hours for full effect.Why you MUST give Vitamin K 10 mg IV at the exact same time as 4F-PCC: 4F-PCC is the parachute for the first 6 hours; IV Vitamin K builds the bridge at hour 6 so the INR does not rebound back up to 5.0 that night ✅ [1][2].Why NEVER forget the 100 kg weight cap, and why NEVER give repeat doses• Why cap weight at 100 kg: Clotting factors stay inside the bloodstream (plasma volume does not double just because a patient weighs 150 kg). Doses above the label maximum and repeat dosing were not studied, and Kcentra carries a Boxed Warning for arterial and venous thromboembolism (stroke, PE, MI), so extra factor adds clot risk without proven benefit ✅ [1].• Contains heparin: Kcentra vials contain a small amount of heparin; it is contraindicated in patients with a history of HIT ✅ [1].Always cap calculation weight at 100 kg (max 2,500 / 3,500 / 5,000 units), pair with Vitamin K 10 mg IV, check HIT history, and recheck INR 30 minutes after infusion ✅ [1][2].
Pharmacist checklist

Which anticoagulant, and when was the last dose?
Current INR and weight (cap at 100 kg).
Vitamin K ordered with it for warfarin.
Any thrombosis in the last 3 months? Weigh the risk.
INR 30 minutes after; no routine repeat dose.

ISMP High Alert Medication (anticoagulant). Boxed warning: spinal and epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture, which can cause permanent paralysis ✅✅ [1][2].

Adult dosing (SC unless noted)




































































IndicationDoseCrCl below 30 mL/minCheckSourcesMedical VTE prophylaxis40 mg once daily30 mg once daily✅✅[1][2]Abdominal surgery prophylaxis40 mg once daily, first dose 2 h before surgery30 mg once daily✅[1]Hip or knee replacement30 mg every 12 h starting 12 to 24 h after surgery (hip alternative: 40 mg daily)30 mg once daily✅[1]DVT or PE treatment1 mg/kg every 12 h, or 1.5 mg/kg once daily (inpatient)1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]Unstable angina / NSTEMI1 mg/kg every 12 h with aspirin1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]STEMI, under 75 years30 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/kg SC, then 1 mg/kg every 12 h (max 100 mg for the first 2 doses)30 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/kg, then 1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]STEMI, 75 years or olderNo IV bolus. 0.75 mg/kg every 12 h (max 75 mg for the first 2 doses)1 mg/kg once daily, no bolus✅✅[1][2]STEMI going to PCILast SC dose under 8 h before balloon: nothing extra. Low body weight (women under 45 kg, men under 57 kg): higher exposure on fixed prophylaxis doses; watch for bleeding ✅ [1].
Obesity (BMI over 30): no consensus on prophylaxis dose adjustment per the label ✅ [1]. Know St. Mary’s obesity protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Enoxaparin is unfractionated heparin chopped into short sugar chains (low molecular weight). Because the chain is short, it still supercharges Antithrombin to block Factor Xa, but its tail is too short to wrap around Factor IIa (thrombin).Because it mainly targets Factor Xa, routine aPTT and PT/INR will NOT measure enoxaparin; if you need a level (renal impairment, pregnancy, obesity, pediatrics), you must order a peak LMWH Anti-Xa level 4 hours after the 3rd dose ✅ [1][2][3].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Peak effect: 3 to 5 hours after SC injection (that is why peak anti Xa is drawn at 4 hours) ✅ [2][3].• Elimination: Cleared almost entirely by the kidneys (unlike unfractionated heparin, which can also be cleared by macrophages and the liver).When CrCl drops below 30 mL/min, enoxaparin stacks up in the blood; you must cut treatment dosing from every 12 hours to once every 24 hours (1 mg/kg once daily) and prophylaxis to 30 mg once daily ✅ [1][2].Why NEVER pull an epidural catheter early, and why Protamine only works ~60%• Spinal hematoma paralysis: Pulling or placing an epidural needle while enoxaparin is active causes bleeding inside the tight bony spinal canal, crushing the spinal cord (Boxed Warning) ✅ [1][2].• Why protamine only reverses ~60%: Protamine binds long negatively charged heparin chains well, but enoxaparin’s short chains slip past it ✅ [1][2].Hold prophylactic enoxaparin 12 hours and treatment enoxaparin 24 hours before neuraxial needle placement or catheter removal, and wait at least 4 hours after removal before the next dose ✅ [2][4].
Monitoring

PT and aPTT do not measure enoxaparin effect ✅ [1].
Anti Xa is used in renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy, children or bleeding ✅✅ [1][2].
Anti Xa targets (treatment): draw a peak about 4 hours after the dose, after the 3rd dose (steady state) ✅✅ [2][3].

1 mg/kg every 12 h: peak 0.5 to 1.0 units/mL ✅ [3]
1.5 mg/kg once daily: peak 1.0 to 2.0 units/mL ✅ [3]
Confirm St. Mary’s lab ranges ⚠️ [VERIFY]


Platelets (HIT risk is lower than with heparin but present), hemoglobin, SCr.

Neuraxial timing (epidural, spinal, catheter)

Prophylactic dose: wait at least 12 hours after the dose before placement or removal ✅✅ [2][4].
Treatment dose (1 mg/kg every 12 h or 1.5 mg/kg daily): wait at least 24 hours ✅✅ [2][4].
After catheter removal: next dose no sooner than 4 hours later ✅ [2].
ASRA updated its guideline after the 2010 edition cited here; check the current edition and St. Mary’s anesthesia policy ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Reversal (protamine)

Enoxaparin given within 8 hours: 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin ✅✅ [1][2].
More than 8 hours, or a second dose needed: 0.5 mg per 1 mg ✅ [1].
12 hours or more since the dose: protamine may not be needed ✅ [1].
Protamine reverses only about 60% of anti Xa activity ✅✅ [1][2].
Max 50 mg per dose ✅ [2]. Risk of hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions; give slowly with resuscitation available ✅ [1].

Contraindications
Active major bleeding; immune mediated HIT within the past 100 days or circulating antibodies; hypersensitivity to enoxaparin, heparin or pork products; benzyl alcohol allergy (multiple dose vials) ✅ [1].
Pediatrics and neonates
Not FDA approved for neonates or infants, though it is used off label with anti Xa monitoring. Multiple dose vials contain benzyl alcohol (gasping syndrome); use single dose syringes ✅ [1]. Pediatric dosing ⚠️ [VERIFY against the pediatric dosing reference St. Mary’s uses].
Pharmacist verification checklist

Indication matches the dose (prophylaxis vs treatment vs ACS).
Weight and CrCl (Cockcroft Gault) both current.
Age 75 or older with STEMI: no bolus, 0.75 mg/kg.
Epidural or spinal planned or in place? Check timing.
Heparin running or given recently? Avoid double anticoagulation.
Platelets, hemoglobin, anti Xa plan if renal, obese or pregnant.

Adult dosing

Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Gentamicin sneaks inside aerobic Gram negative bacteria (using an oxygen powered door) and locks onto the 30S ribosome, forcing the bacteria to print scrambled, toxic proteins until the cell dies. Why one big dose works (7 mg/kg): It is concentration dependent (higher peak = faster kill) and has a post antibiotic effect (bacteria stay stunned for hours even after serum gentamicin drops to zero).Giving one large dose (7 mg/kg) gets a high peak to kill Gram negative rods, and then gives the kidneys and inner ear a drug free holiday for the second half of the day ✅ [2][3].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Distribution (Vd ≈ 0.3 L/kg in adults, larger in neonates): Stays mostly in extracellular water ✅ [3].• Elimination: Cleared 100% unchanged by the kidneys.Why low troughs (< 2 mcg/mL traditional, or drug free interval on Hartford) save the kidneys and ears: kidney proximal tubule cells and inner ear hair cells saturate when they take up gentamicin; they only get poisoned when the drug sits around continuously 24 hours a day without a trough holiday ✅ [1][2].Why NEVER use Hartford nomogram for a 3 mg/kg dose, and why gentamicin NEVER kills anaerobes alone• Never plot a non 7 mg/kg dose on the Hartford chart: The Hartford nomogram lines were mathematically drawn only for a 7 mg/kg dose; plotting a 5 mg/kg or 3 mg/kg level on that graph gives a completely wrong interval ✅ [3].• Why it never covers anaerobes: The door that pulls gentamicin inside a bacterium requires oxygen; anaerobic bacteria don’t use oxygen, so gentamicin is locked out.Always verify that a Hartford level came from a 7 mg/kg dose drawn between 6 and 14 hours after the start of the infusion, and avoid stacking loop diuretics or other nephrotoxins ✅ [1][3].
Pharmacist checklist

Which method: traditional or extended interval?
Weight (actual vs adjusted), SCr and urine output.
Level ordered at the right time.
Avoid with other nephrotoxins where possible; baseline hearing complaints.
Duration: label usual 7 to 10 days ✅ [1].

Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Think of Antithrombin III as the body’s natural police officer that handcuffs clotting factors (Factor IIa [thrombin] and Factor Xa). By itself, Antithrombin walks slowly. Unfractionated heparin straps a jetpack onto Antithrombin so it handcuffs clotting factors 1,000 times faster. Because unfractionated heparin has a long sugar tail, it can wrap around both Factor Xa and Factor IIa.Because it blocks thrombin immediately, it stops existing clots from growing right away while the body dissolves them ✅ [5].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• IV bolus onset: Immediate.• Half life: 30 to 90 minutes (dose dependent: higher doses saturate clearance and last longer) ✅ [5][6].• Steady state after rate change: 6 hours ✅ [4].That 30 to 90 minute half life is why surgeons love IV heparin in the ICU (turn the pump off and the effect fades in a few hours) and why you check aPTT or anti Xa 6 hours after every rate change ✅ [4][5].Why NEVER bolus after recent Enoxaparin, and why NEVER give benzyl alcohol vials to babies• No bolus on top of Enoxaparin: If the patient received treatment dose enoxaparin within the last 12 hours, their Factor Xa is already blocked; giving a full heparin bolus on top causes major hemorrhage ✅ [4].• No benzyl alcohol in neonates: Multi dose heparin vials preserved with benzyl alcohol cause fatal neonatal gasping syndrome (metabolic acidosis and respiratory collapse) ✅ [5].• Why heparin raises K+: Heparin suppresses aldosterone in the adrenal gland after several days, causing the kidneys to hold onto potassium ✅ [5].Always check the MAR for prior enoxaparin before verifying a heparin bolus, always use preservative free syringes in neonates, and watch serum K+ when therapy runs over 5 days ✅ [4][5].
Safety (why it’s high alert)

Look alike strengths: 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 units/mL vials look alike. Fatal pediatric hemorrhages have happened when 1 mL heparin vials were confused with 1 mL catheter lock flush vials (FDA label section 5.1) ✅ [5].
Use premixed bags and smart pump libraries for infusions.
Contraindicated with a history of HIT, uncontrolled active bleeding (except DIC), and when coagulation tests can’t be done at appropriate intervals ✅ [5].

Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

Use the 4Ts score to estimate pretest probability; with a low 4Ts score, don’t send HIT testing and don’t treat empirically (strong recommendation) ✅ [7] ASH 2018.
If HIT is suspected (intermediate or high 4Ts): stop all heparin (including flushes and heparin coated catheters) and start a non heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC (conditional) ✅ [7].
Argatroban: 2 mcg/kg/min; 0.5 mcg/kg/min in moderate or severe hepatic impairment; max 10 mcg/kg/min; aPTT 1.5 to 3 times baseline (not above 100 seconds), check 2 hours after starting or changing ✅ [8] FDA label.
Warfarin overlap with argatroban: no loading dose; stop argatroban when INR is above 4 on combined therapy (at argatroban 2 mcg/kg/min or less), recheck INR in 4 to 6 hours ✅ [8].
Start warfarin only after platelets recover (at least 150,000), with overlap; ASH 2018 prefers a DOAC when appropriate; treat 3 to 6 months with thrombosis, about 4 to 6 weeks without ✅ The Blood Project: switching off argatroban in HIT (ASH 2018).

Pharmacist verification checklist

Indication and the right nomogram (VTE vs ACS vs low intensity).
Dosing weight (actual body weight; know St. Mary’s cap for obesity).
Baseline aPTT or anti Xa, CBC, platelets, SCr.
Any enoxaparin in the last 12 hours? (Don’t bolus) ✅ [4]
Concentration and bag match the pump library.
Lab draw times ordered.

Insulin, IV (DKA and HHS, adults) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s DKA order set before clinical use.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication. Use the standard concentration in the smart pump library and an independent double check.
DKA diagnosis (2024 consensus)
All three: D glucose 200 mg/dL or higher, or known diabetes at any glucose (catches euglycemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors); K beta hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or higher (or urine ketones 2+); A pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 ✅✅ [1][2].
Dosing



























































ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesSevere DKAFixed rate IV regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; no routine bolus (0.1 units/kg bolus only if IV access is delayed)✅✅[1][2]HHS0.05 units/kg/h (treat as DKA if ketotic or acidotic)✅✅[1][2]Potassium below 3.5Hold insulin. Give potassium about 10 mmol/h until K is above 3.5✅✅[1][2]Potassium 3.5 to 5.0Add 10 to 20 mmol K per liter of fluid; goal K 4 to 5✅✅[1][2]Potassium above 5.0No potassium; recheck every 2 h✅[1]Glucose below 250Add D5 or D10; lower DKA insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h; keep insulin running until ketones clear✅✅[1][2]Glucose goal during DKA treatment150 to 200 mg/dL (HHS 200 to 250)✅[1]Mild or uncomplicated moderate DKASC rapid acting insulin every 1 to 2 h is an accepted alternative✅✅[1][2]
Change from older teaching: the 2009 statement used K 3.3 as the cutoff and allowed a 0.1 units/kg bolus. The 2024 consensus uses 3.5 and no routine bolus ✅ [1]. Pediatric DKA follows ISPAD 2022 (see PICU_Core).
Potassium decision path before starting insulin
flowchart TD

    Decision -->|"Below 3.5"| Red["HOLD INSULIN<br/>Give potassium about 10 mmol/h<br/>until K is above 3.5 ✅✅ [1][2]"]
    Decision -->|"3.5 to 5.0"| Amber["ADD POTASSIUM + START INSULIN<br/>Add 10 to 20 mmol K per liter of fluid (goal K 4 to 5)<br/>Fixed rate IV regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/h ✅✅ [1][2]"]
    Decision -->|"Above 5.0"| Green["START INSULIN ONLY<br/>No potassium; recheck every 2 h<br/>Fixed rate IV regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/h ✅ <a href="doi.org/10.2337/dci24-0032" target="_blank" rel="noopener" class="ref">[1]</a>"]
    Red -->|"Once K is above 3.5"| Amber

    style Decision fill:#334155,stroke:#64748b,color:#f8fafc
    style Red fill:#991b1b,stroke:#dc2626,color:#ffffff
    style Amber fill:#92400e,stroke:#d97706,color:#ffffff
    style Green fill:#166534,stroke:#16a34a,color:#ffffff

Sources: Umpierrez GE et al., Diabetes Care 2024 consensus report [1][2] ✅✅

How it works in the body (plain English for fast recall)

Why potassium comes before insulin (the two door rule): Think of insulin as a key that opens two doors on every cell at the same time: one door pulls sugar (glucose) out of the blood into the cell, and a second door (the sodium potassium pump) pulls potassium out of the blood into the cell. In DKA, acid in the blood has pushed potassium out of the cells, and high urine output has washed potassium out of the body. If serum potassium is already below 3.5 and you turn on an insulin drip, insulin pushes the remaining potassium out of the blood into the cells, and serum potassium drops to a level that can cause dangerous heart rhythms. That is why you hold insulin and give potassium (about 10 mmol/h) until K is above 3.5 ✅✅ [1][2].
Why you add dextrose when glucose falls below 250 (clear the acid, not just the sugar): Blood glucose drops much faster than blood ketones (acid) clear. When glucose reaches below 250 mg/dL, do not turn off the insulin drip, because the body still needs insulin to shut off ketone production. Instead, add D5 or D10 to the IV fluids to prevent hypoglycemia and lower the DKA insulin drip to 0.05 units/kg/h until ketones clear ✅✅ [1][2].
Timing in the body (why basal insulin goes in 1 to 2 hours before stopping the drip): IV regular insulin starts working within minutes, and once you stop the pump its effect fades within 30 to 60 minutes. Subcutaneous basal insulin takes 1 to 2 hours to absorb and take over. Giving subcutaneous basal insulin at least 1 to 2 hours before stopping the IV drip prevents a gap with zero insulin in the body, which would let ketone production rebound ✅✅ [1][2].

Fluids
Isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid 500 to 1,000 mL/h for 2 to 4 h if heart and kidneys allow; smaller boluses in older adults and heart or kidney failure ✅ [1].
Resolution and transition

DKA resolved: beta hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L and pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher ✅ [1].
Give basal insulin at least 1 to 2 hours before stopping the drip ✅✅ [1][2]. Estimate total daily dose 0.3 to 0.6 units/kg/day ✅✅ [1][2].

Monitoring
K at baseline, 2 h after insulin starts, then every 4 h; glucose hourly ✅ [1].
Pharmacist checklist

K result before insulin starts.
No bolus unless IV delay.
Dextrose added at glucose below 250.
SGLT2 inhibitor on home list? Hold it.
Basal insulin ordered 1 to 2 h before the drip stops.

Sources

Umpierrez GE, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: consensus report. Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 · summary: Hyperglycemic crises in adults: a look at the 2024 consensus report. Cleve Clin J Med. 2025;92(3):152-158

Preeclampsia and eclampsia

Sources: Magnesium Sulfate in 5% Dextrose FDA label (Hospira 2019) [1]; UT Southwestern CME 2026 [2].
Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Calcium is the “spark” that makes nerves fire acetylcholine and muscles contract. Magnesium is calcium’s calm twin brother: it sits inside the calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction and brain synapses so nerves stop misfiring into eclampsia seizures.Why Calcium Gluconate is the antidote: When magnesium climbs too high and paralyzes the diaphragm, 1 g IV calcium gluconate floods the synapse with calcium to push magnesium off the receptors so the patient can breathe again ✅ [1][2].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• IV loading dose (4 to 6 g over 15 to 20 min): Reaches seizure preventing levels immediately.• IM option: Takes about 60 minutes for onset.• Elimination: 100% cleared by the kidneys in the urine.Because ONLY the kidneys clear magnesium, if urine output drops below 100 mL over 4 hours (or SCr rises), the maintenance drip will rapidly build up to toxic levels (> 4 to 10 mEq/L) ✅ [1][2].Why NEVER push fast, why NEVER run over 5 to 7 days in pregnancy, and why NEVER give in myasthenia gravis• Never push fast: Rapid IV bolus causes severe flushing, hypotension, and cardiac conduction block.• Never run past 5 to 7 days in pregnancy: Pulls calcium out of the baby’s developing bones, causing fetal hypocalcemia and neonatal bone fractures ✅ [1][2].• Never give in myasthenia gravis: Those patients barely have working acetylcholine receptors; blocking calcium release triggers instant respiratory failure ✅ [1].Always infuse the loading dose over 15 to 20 minutes on a dedicated pump channel, cap therapy at 24 hours postpartum, and keep calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) at the bedside ✅ [1][2].
Monitoring and toxicity

Check patellar reflexes, respiratory rate (concern below about 16 per label), urine output (keep at least 100 mL per 4 h; stop if lower, especially with rising SCr), serum magnesium ✅✅ [1][2].
Label levels: reflexes weaken above about 4 mEq/L; respiratory paralysis risk at about 10 mEq/L ✅ [1]. Eclampsia target per label 2.5 to 5 mEq/L (3 to 6 mg/dL) ✅ [1].
Antidote: stop the infusion; calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over about 3 minutes; support breathing. Have calcium at the bedside before starting ✅✅ [1][2].
Contraindications: heart block or myocardial damage, myasthenia gravis ✅ [1]. Don’t combine with nifedipine or terbutaline per label caution ✅ [1].
Newborns of treated mothers may need resuscitation and calcium ✅ [1].

Other uses (not in the preeclampsia label)

Torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemic arrest: 1 to 2 g IV ✅ (see Codes_Resuscitation).
Fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks: per L&D protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].
Hypomagnesemia repletion: per St. Mary’s electrolyte protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Norepinephrine · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s vasopressor titration protocol and pump library.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication (adrenergic agonist).







































































ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesRole in septic shockFirst line vasopressor✅✅[2] SSC 2021; [3] SSC summaryMAP target65 mmHg✅✅[2][3]Label starting rate8 to 12 mcg/min, then titrate; usual maintenance 2 to 4 mcg/min✅[1]Weight based dosing (mcg/kg/min)Many ICUs use it⚠️[VERIFY St. Mary’s units]Add vasopressinWhen MAP is inadequate on low to moderate norepinephrine✅[2]Peripheral startReasonable short term in a proximal vein above the antecubital fossa while central access is placed✅[2]Cardiac dysfunction with poor perfusionConsider adding dobutamine or switching to epinephrine✅[2]ExtravasationPhentolamine 5 to 10 mg in 10 to 15 mL NS, infiltrated into the area as soon as possible (works best within 12 h)✅[1]Premixed bags4 mg/250 mL (16 mcg/mL), 8 mg/250 mL (32 mcg/mL), 16 mg/250 mL (64 mcg/mL) in NS✅[1]Infusion siteLarge vein; avoid leg veins in elderly or vascular disease✅[1]
Drip math
At 16 mcg/mL, 5 mcg/min = 0.31 mL/min = about 18.8 mL/h. (See Codes_Resuscitation and IV prep notes.)

Sources: Norepinephrine FDA label (2022) [1]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 [2][3].
Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)In septic shock, blood vessels go limp like a wide open garden hose, so blood pressure crashes. Norepinephrine strongly squeezes Alpha-1 (α1) receptors on artery walls (tightening the nozzle so pressure rises to a MAP of 65 mmHg) and gently nudges Beta-1 (β1) receptors on the heart so cardiac output stays steady without racing the heart as fast as epinephrine or dopamine.First line vasopressor in septic shock; when norepinephrine climbs to low or moderate doses and MAP is still below 65 mmHg, add vasopressin (which squeezes a completely different receptor, V1) ✅ [2][3].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Onset: 1 to 2 minutes IV.• Duration after stopping: 1 to 2 minutes (broken down almost instantly by COMT and MAO enzymes).Because it wears off in 1 to 2 minutes, never let the IV bag run dry; prepare the replacement bag before the current bag empties or the patient’s blood pressure will bottom out in 60 seconds.Why NEVER run in a tiny hand/leg vein, and why Phentolamine saves the skin• Why extravasation kills tissue: If norepinephrine leaks out of a small vein into the skin, its powerful Alpha-1 squeeze shuts off 100% of blood flow to that skin patch, turning it white, cold, and necrotic ✅ [1].• Why Phentolamine works: Phentolamine is a direct Alpha-1 blocker; injecting 5 to 10 mg in 10 to 15 mL NS under the skin unlocks the clamped blood vessels and restores pink blood flow ✅ [1].Avoid leg veins or tiny hand veins; if started peripherally, use a large vein above the antecubital fossa while a central line is placed, and know where phentolamine is stocked ✅ [1][2].
Pharmacist checklist

Concentration matches the pump library entry.
Units: mcg/min vs mcg/kg/min.
Line: central, or peripheral with a time limit and site checks.
Phentolamine available.
Volume status addressed (fluids first in sepsis).

Sources

FDA label, Norepinephrine Bitartrate in Sodium Chloride (2022)
SCCM: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, vasoactive agents infographic
Evans L, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. Crit Care Med 2021;49:e1063-e1143 · summary: EMdocs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 updates

Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)98% of the body’s potassium lives inside the cells, and only 2% floats in the bloodstream. That tiny 2% sets the electrical resting voltage of the heart muscle. Why Magnesium matters: Magnesium acts as the “plug” in the kidney’s distal tubule potassium channels (ROMK). Without magnesium, the kidney drain stays wide open and every bag of potassium you infuse pours straight into the urine.Always check and replace magnesium alongside potassium in hypokalemic patients ✅ [Huang and Kuo 2007].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Expected rise: Every 20 mEq of IV KCl raises serum K+ by roughly 0.25 mEq/L (so 40 mEq raises K+ by about 0.4 to 0.5 mEq/L if kidneys and acid base are stable) ✅ [2].• Infusion duration: Because peripheral veins max out at 10 mEq/h, a 40 mEq total replacement takes 4 hours peripherally ✅ [1][2].Do not recheck a serum potassium level 5 minutes after the bag finishes; allow equilibration and make sure the nurse does not draw the lab upstream from the arm infusing potassium.Why NEVER give IV push, and why NEVER run >10 mEq/h in a peripheral vein• Why IV push is fatal: Pushing concentrated KCl hits the heart all at once before it can enter cells, erasing the heart’s electrical gradient and stopping the heart in diastole ✅ [1].• Why peripheral veins burn above 10 mEq/h: Potassium is a strong chemical irritant (caustic/vesicant at high concentrations); running > 10 mEq/h or 40 mEq/100 mL in a small hand/arm vein burns the vein wall and causes severe tissue necrosis if it extravasates ✅ [1].Peripheral max = 10 mEq/h. Anything faster than 10 mEq/h or concentrated 40 mEq/100 mL bags must go through a central line with continuous telemetry ✅ [1][2].
Pharmacist checklist

Rate at or below 10 mEq/h peripherally.
Central line and telemetry for anything faster.
Renal function and urine output before repleting.
Not running with other potassium sources (TPN, maintenance fluids) without a total count.
DKA: K below 3.5 means potassium first, insulin held (Insulin_IV_DKA).

FDA label, Potassium Chloride Injection (highly concentrated, 2019)
