drug-hub/monographs/thrombolytics_stroke.content:
Tenecteplase and Alteplase (acute ischemic stroke) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s stroke alert order set.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication (thrombolytics). Look alike names and packaging: alteplase vs tenecteplase, and stroke dose vs cardiac dose.
Dosing





























AgentStroke doseCheckSourcesTenecteplase0.25 mg/kg actual body weight, max 25 mg, single IV bolus over 5 seconds, then NS flush (not dextrose compatible)✅✅[1] SUNY Downstate pharmacy update 2025; [2] AHA/ASA 2026 summary; FDA approval for stroke March 2025 [3]Tenecteplase cardiac (STEMI) bands, for contrastunder 60 kg 30 mg; 60 to 69 kg 35 mg; 70 to 79 kg 40 mg; 80 to 89 kg 45 mg; 90 kg or more 50 mg✅[1]Alteplase0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes✅✅[1]; [4] Stroke module sources
2026 AHA/ASA guideline: tenecteplase is equally preferred to alteplase; window up to 4.5 h, or up to 9 h in selected patients by imaging ✅✅ [2][5].
Key contraindications (bleeding risk)
Prior or current intracranial hemorrhage; ischemic stroke, head trauma or intracranial surgery within 3 months; SAH; GI bleed or GI cancer within 21 days; aortic dissection; endocarditis; platelets below 100,000; INR above 1.7; treatment dose enoxaparin within 24 h; recent DOAC; heparin with aPTT above 40 s ✅ [1]. (Full list: St. Mary’s order set.)
Around the dose

BP below 185/110 before; below 180/105 for 24 h after ✅ (see Stroke_Core).
No antithrombotics for 24 h after.
Angioedema and bleeding management: see Stroke_Core.

Sources: SUNY Downstate 2025 [1]; AHA/ASA 2026 summary [2][5]; FDA stroke approval March 2025 [3]; Stroke_Core [4].
Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)A stroke clot is held together by a tight net of fibrin threads. Both tenecteplase and alteplase bind to fibrin inside the clot and turn plasminogen into plasmin (molecular scissors that cut the fibrin net apart). Why Tenecteplase is a 5 second push: Tenecteplase was bioengineered at 3 spots (T-N-K) so it locks onto fibrin more tightly and resists breakdown (PAI-1), giving it a longer half life that works as a single 5 second IV push instead of a 1 hour drip.In the 2026 AHA/ASA guidelines, tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) is equally preferred to alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) ✅ [2][5].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Alteplase plasma half life: About 5 minutes (which is why 90% of the dose must be infused continuously over 60 minutes) ✅ [1].• Tenecteplase plasma half life: About 20 to 24 minutes (which allows a single 5 second IV push) ✅ [1].• Fibrinogen depletion window: Lasts up to 24 hours (which is why all blood thinners and aspirin are held for 24 hours after the dose) ✅ [1][4].Document the exact bolus time and ensure no antithrombotics (no aspirin, heparin, or enoxaparin) are ordered for the next 24 hours until the repeat head CT clears ✅ [1][4].Why NEVER use the 50 mg STEMI vial without wasting excess, and why NEVER mix Tenecteplase with Dextrose• Stroke max is 25 mg (half the cardiac max of 50 mg): Pushing a 40 or 50 mg cardiac STEMI dose into a stroke patient’s fragile brain vessels causes fatal intracranial hemorrhage ✅ [1].• Never flush Tenecteplase with Dextrose (D5W): Tenecteplase precipitates (turns cloudy) on contact with dextrose lines; always flush the line with 0.9% Normal Saline (NS) before and after the push ✅ [1].Draw up only the calculated stroke dose (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) into the syringe, waste the remainder of the vial before handing it to the nurse, and flush with NS only ✅ [1].
Pharmacist checklist

Which agent? Read the vial name twice.
Weight: measured or estimated; stroke dose, not cardiac.
Tenecteplase: draw up only the stroke dose and discard the rest per policy.
Anticoagulant history and last dose time.
Document bolus time.

Vancomycin (IV) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s pharmacy to dose protocol and its dosing software.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Dosing and monitoring (2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP consensus, serious MRSA)

































































ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesTargetAUC 400 to 600 mg·h/L (assuming MIC 1)✅✅[1][2]Trough only monitoringNot recommended✅✅[1][2]How to get AUCBayesian software (preferred) or two levels (one 1 to 2 h after infusion, one trough)✅✅[1][2]Loading dose (critically ill)20 to 35 mg/kg actual body weight, max 3,000 mg✅✅[1][2]Pediatrics 3 months to 12 years60 to 80 mg/kg/day divided every 6 h; same AUC target✅[1]Pediatrics 12 years and older60 to 70 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 h✅[1]Pediatric empiric max3,600 mg/day (normal kidneys)✅[1]Maintenance (adults)15 to 20 mg/kg actual body weight every 8 to 12 h, then adjust to AUC; children 3 months and older 60 to 80 mg/kg/day divided q6 to 8h✅✅Consultant360: 2020 vancomycin guideline; US Pharmacist: optimizing vancomycin (2023)NeonatesAUC guided where possible; use the neonatal dosing reference⚠️see NICU_Core
Safety

Higher AUC (above 600) and troughs above 15 to 20 raise acute kidney injury risk; watch with piperacillin tazobactam, contrast, loop diuretics ⚠️ [VERIFY second source].
Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly “red man syndrome”): slow the infusion (at least 60 minutes, max 10 mg/min for doses over 500 mg; 90 to 120 min after a prior reaction); antihistamine. It’s not a true allergy ✅ RCH Melbourne: vancomycin IV guideline.

Sources: 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP Vancomycin Consensus Guideline (Rybak et al. 2020) [1][2]; RCH Melbourne IV guideline.
Plain English memory guide: Mechanism, body timing, and “why never”

























ConceptPlain English pictureClinical rule on shiftHow it works (Mechanism)Bacteria build their cell wall out of bricks that end in two little hooks (D-Ala-D-Ala). Whereas beta lactams break the trowel (PBP enzyme) that lays the bricks, vancomycin is a giant steel cap that snaps directly over the D-Ala-D-Ala bricks themselves so MRSA cannot glue its wall together. Because vancomycin is a huge molecule, it cannot squeeze through the outer membrane of Gram negative bacteria (Gram positive only).Vancomycin kills slowly and depends on total 24 hour exposure (AUC/MIC target 400 to 600) rather than a single high peak ✅ [1][2].How long it takes in the body (Body Timing)• Loading dose (20 to 35 mg/kg actual weight, max 3,000 mg): Fills the patient’s fluid volume (Vd) on Day 1 so critically ill patients don’t wait 24 to 36 hours to reach therapeutic levels ✅ [1][2].• Elimination: Cleared >80 to 90% unchanged by the kidneys.Why the 2020 guideline dropped trough only (15 to 20 mcg/mL) monitoring: many patients hit an AUC of 400 to 600 at a trough of only 11 or 12 mcg/mL; pushing their trough to 18 mcg/mL gave them an AUC over 700 and injured their kidneys ✅ [1][2].Why NEVER infuse faster than 10 mg/min, and why IV vancomycin NEVER treats C. diff• Why fast infusions cause flushing (“Vancomycin Infusion Reaction”): Infusing faster than 10 mg/min directly pokes mast cells in the skin to dump histamine (bright red neck/chest and itching). It is a rate reaction, NOT a true IgE allergy ✅ [RCH Melbourne].• Why IV vancomycin fails in C. diff: Vancomycin is too large to cross from the bloodstream into the colon lumen (and oral vancomycin stays in the gut and never reaches the blood for pneumonia/bacteremia; see ID_Core).FDA label: infuse over at least 60 min and no faster than 10 mg/min, whichever is longer (1,000 mg = 100 min, 1,500 mg = 150 min, 2,000 mg = 200 min). Many hospitals use a faster 1 g per hour protocol; follow St. Mary’s infusion policy ⚠️; if flushing occurs, pause, give diphenhydramine, and restart slower over 90 to 120 minutes ✅.
Pharmacist checklist

Indication and whether a loading dose is needed.
Actual body weight; SCr trend; urine output.
Level plan (Bayesian or two levels), not trough only.
Nephrotoxic combinations.
Infusion time matches dose.

Sources

Rybak MJ, et al. Vancomycin therapeutic monitoring consensus. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2020;77:835-864 · summary: Pharmacy Times: New guidelines released for monitoring vancomycin in serious MRSA infections (summarizes Rybak MJ, et al. Am J Health Syst Pharm. 2020;77(11):835-864)

journal-club/jc_act.content:
Journal Club: AcT (tenecteplase vs alteplase for stroke)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Stroke_Core · Drug: Thrombolytics_Stroke
0. 60 second bottom line

“AcT (Lancet 2022) randomized 1,600 thrombolysis eligible stroke patients within 4.5 hours at 22 Canadian centers to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg. Excellent outcome (mRS 0 to 1 at 90 to 120 days) was 36.9% vs 34.8% (difference 2.1%, 95% CI minus 2.6 to 6.9), meeting the minus 5% noninferiority margin. Symptomatic ICH (3.4% vs 3.2%) and death (15.3% vs 15.4%) were similar. The main limitation is open label treatment. For our patients, tenecteplase is a one bolus option with the same results, and the dose must be the stroke dose, not the cardiac dose.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Menon BK, Buck BH, Singh N, et al. Lancet 2022;400(10347):161-169 ✅ McMaster Optimal Aging: AcT citation. Pragmatic, registry linked.
2. PICO





























PopulationAdults 18 or older, ischemic stroke within 4.5 h, eligible for thrombolysis; mean age 74, 48% female ✅ [1]InterventionTenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, max 25 mg ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorAlteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg (10% bolus, 90% over 60 min) ✅✅ [1][2]OutcomesPrimary: mRS 0 to 1 at 90 to 120 days. Safety: symptomatic ICH at 24 h, 90 day deathDesignNoninferiority, open label, blinded outcome assessment, margin minus 5% ✅✅ [1][2]
3. Validity

Strengths: real world, large, blinded outcome assessors, both ITT style and safety analyses.
Red flags: open label; telephone outcome assessment; few primary stroke centers; daytime only enrollment at some sites ✅ [2].
Noninferiority check: margin stated and met; the whole CI sits above minus 5%.

4. Results

































OutcomeTenecteplaseAlteplaseEffectCheckmRS 0 to 136.9% (296/802)34.8% (266/765)Difference 2.1% (minus 2.6 to 6.9)✅✅ [1][2]Symptomatic ICH, 24 h3.4%3.2%Similar✅✅ [1][2]90 day death15.3%15.4%Similar✅ [2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Single bolus helps with transfers and drip and ship. Our biggest risk is the dose: tenecteplase cardiac (STEMI) dosing uses weight bands up to 50 mg. See Thrombolytics_Stroke.
6. Role in therapy
“For eligible ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is a reasonable first line alternative to alteplase; AHA/ASA 2026 lists it as equally preferred.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Confirm the stroke dose and the max of 25 mg.
Check the weight band chart and the vial.
Same BP and antithrombotic rules as alteplase.

Sources

journal-club/jc_bridge.title: JC_BRIDGE
journal-club/jc_bridge.content:
Journal Club: BRIDGE (bridging warfarin around surgery in AF)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Anticoagulation_Core · Drug: Enoxaparin
0. 60 second bottom line

“BRIDGE (NEJM 2015) randomized 1,884 patients with atrial fibrillation on warfarin who stopped it 5 days before elective surgery to dalteparin 100 IU/kg SC twice daily or placebo as a bridge. Arterial clots were 0.4% with no bridge vs 0.3% with bridging, meeting noninferiority. Major bleeding was 1.3% vs 3.2% (p 0.005; NNH about 53 for bridging). The main limitation is that few very high stroke risk patients and no mechanical valves were included. For our AF patients on warfarin, don’t bridge.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Douketis JD, Spyropoulos AC, Kaatz S, et al. N Engl J Med 2015;373(9):823-833. NCT00786474. NHLBI funded ✅✅ [1][2]. Before BRIDGE, bridging was common practice with little trial evidence.
2. PICO





























PopulationAdults with chronic AF or flutter on warfarin at least 3 months (INR 2 to 3) with at least one CHADS2 risk factor, having elective surgery. Excluded: stroke or TIA in the past 12 weeks, major bleeding in 6 weeks, CrCl below 30, platelets below 100,000, cardiac, intracranial or spinal surgery ✅ [2]InterventionDalteparin 100 IU/kg SC BID from 3 days before until about 24 h before surgery; restarted 12 to 24 h (low bleed risk) or 48 to 72 h (high bleed risk) after, until INR 2 or more ✅ [1]ComparatorMatched placeboOutcomesEfficacy: arterial thromboembolism at 37 days. Safety: major bleedingDesignRandomized, double blind, placebo controlled, noninferiority ✅✅ [1][2]
3. Validity

Strengths: double blind and placebo controlled (rare for a bridging study); clear protocol.
Red flags: event rate lower than planned; mean CHADS2 was moderate, so very high risk patients were underrepresented ⚠️ [VERIFY mean CHADS2]; mechanical valves not studied.

4. Results








































OutcomeNo bridgeBridgeEffectCheckArterial thromboembolism0.4% (4)0.3% (3)Noninferior✅✅ [1][2]Major bleeding1.3% (12)3.2% (29)p 0.005; ARI 1.9%, NNH about 53✅✅ [1][2]Minor bleeding12.0%20.9%p below 0.001✅ [2]Death, MI, DVT, PENo difference✅ [2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Matches CHEST 2022: strong recommendation against bridging in AF. Mechanical valves and recent clots are a different question; follow cardiology and St. Mary’s policy (Anticoagulation_Core).
6. Role in therapy
“For patients with AF on warfarin having elective surgery, stop warfarin 5 days before and don’t bridge with LMWH.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Catch reflexive enoxaparin bridge orders for AF (Cases_Anticoag_and_Verification, simulator case 18).
Restart warfarin the evening of or day after surgery at the usual dose ✅ [1].

Sources

Douketis JD, et al. Perioperative bridging in AF (BRIDGE). N Engl J Med 2015;373:823-833 · summary: NHLBI BioLINCC: BRIDGE study

journal-club/jc_crash-2.title: JC_CRASH-2
journal-club/jc_crash-2.content:
Journal Club: CRASH-2 (TXA in trauma)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Trauma_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010) randomized 20,211 bleeding or at risk adult trauma patients within 8 hours of injury to tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, or placebo. 28 day all cause death was 14.5% vs 16.0% (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97; ARR 1.5%, NNT 67). The main limitation is that benefit depends on timing: a later analysis found harm when TXA started more than 3 hours after injury. For our trauma patients, TXA goes in within 3 hours or not at all.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
CRASH-2 collaborators. Lancet 2010;376(9734):23-32. 274 hospitals, 40 countries. Before CRASH-2, TXA had surgical data but no large trauma trial. ✅ [1]
2. PICO





























PopulationAdults within 8 h of injury with significant bleeding or at risk (SBP below 90 and/or HR above 110, or clinician judgment) ✅ [1]InterventionTXA 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorMatched placeboOutcomesPrimary: death in hospital within 4 weeks. Secondary: vascular occlusive events, transfusion, surgeryDesignDouble blind, placebo controlled, superiority
3. Validity: strengths and red flags

Strengths: very large, blinded, placebo controlled, simple outcome (death).
Red flags: cause of death and clot events judged by sites (misclassification likely); transfusion and surgery were similar between groups, so how it works is unclear; mostly low and middle income settings. ✅ [1]

4. Results





































OutcomeTXAPlaceboEffectARR / NNTCheckAll cause death14.5%16.0%RR 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97)1.5% / 67✅✅ [1][2]Death due to bleeding4.9%5.7%RR 0.85 (0.76 to 0.96)0.8% / 125✅✅ [1][2]Any vascular occlusive event1.7%2.0%RR 0.84 (0.68 to 1.02), not significant✅ [1]
Timing (exploratory, Roberts 2011), death due to bleeding: within 1 h RR 0.68; 1 to 3 h RR 0.79; after 3 h RR 1.44 (harm). ✅ [1]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Level I trauma center: TXA belongs in the trauma bay and massive transfusion workflow, with the clock started at injury, not arrival. Ask “Did EMS already give TXA?” to avoid a duplicate load.
6. Role in therapy
“For adult trauma patients with significant bleeding, TXA 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours is reasonable first line if started within 3 hours of injury; after 3 hours it is not recommended.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Check the time of injury before verifying.
Second gram runs over 8 hours: make sure the infusion is actually ordered.
Label renal adjustment (SCr 1.36 to 2.83: 10 mg/kg BID; 2.83 to 5.66: daily; above 5.66: q48h) is for repeated dosing; trauma practice gives the standard load ✅✅ Cyklokapron US label (Drugs.com); Cyklokapron SmPC (UK) (trauma load ⚠️ protocol).
Seizures are linked to high doses (cardiac surgery) and wrong route; IV only, never neuraxial (fatal); label TXA syringes clearly ✅✅ Cyklokapron US label (Drugs.com); Cyklokapron SmPC (UK).

Sources

CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Tranexamic acid in bleeding trauma patients. Lancet 2010;376:23-32 · summary: Critical Care Reviews: CRASH-2
RCEMLearning: CRASH-2 trial
LSHTM research online: CRASH-2 paper

journal-club/jc_esett.title: JC_ESETT
journal-club/jc_esett.content:
Journal Club: ESETT (second line drugs for status epilepticus)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: PICU_Core · Codes_Resuscitation
0. 60 second bottom line

“ESETT (NEJM 2019) randomized children and adults with benzodiazepine refractory convulsive status epilepticus to levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg over 10 minutes. Seizures stopped with improved responsiveness at 60 minutes in 47%, 45% and 46%: no meaningful difference. Safety was similar, with numerically more hypotension and intubation with fosphenytoin. The main limitation is early stopping and unblinding. For our ED and PICU, any of the three is acceptable second line, so pick by patient factors.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Kapur J, et al. N Engl J Med 2019;381(22):2103-2113 ✅ PubMed 31774955. NIH funded ✅ [1]. Before ESETT, second line choice had little head to head evidence.
2. PICO

























PopulationAge 2 and older with convulsive status epilepticus despite adequate benzodiazepines; 57 US EDs ✅ [1]Intervention and comparators (all over 10 min)Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4,500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1,500 mg PE); valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3,000 mg) ✅✅ [1][2]OutcomeSeizure cessation and improved responsiveness at 60 min without more anticonvulsantsDesignBlinded, response adaptive, stopped early for futility (384 analyzed in the three arms) ✅✅ [1][2]
3. Validity

Strengths: blinded, head to head, pragmatic ED setting.
Red flags: stopped early; 23% to 33% per group did not meet eligibility; unblinding in about half of enrollments; mixed children and adults; responsiveness is subjective ✅✅ [1][2].

4. Results















































OutcomeLevetiracetamFosphenytoinValproateCheckPrimary success47%45%46%✅✅ [1][2]Probability of being best0.410.240.35✅ [2]Life threatening hypotension0.7%3.2%1.6%✅✅ [1][2]Intubation within 60 min20%26%17%✅✅ [1][2]Death4.7%2.4%1.6%✅✅ [1][2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Children’s hospital and adult ED both apply (age 2 and up). Choose by patient: valproate avoided in pregnancy, liver disease and suspected mitochondrial disease; fosphenytoin needs cardiac monitoring; levetiracetam needs renal adjustment for maintenance.
6. Role in therapy
“For benzodiazepine refractory status epilepticus, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate are equally effective second line options; choose by patient factors.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Check weight and the max dose for each drug.
Fosphenytoin is dosed in PE; max rate 150 mg PE/min in adults, and in children 2 mg PE/kg/min or 150 mg PE/min, whichever is slower; monitor ECG and BP during and 10 to 20 min after ✅ Fosphenytoin label (Hikma, via Janusinfo).
Valproate: pregnancy, liver, and age under 2 risks.
Have the third line (anesthetic infusion) ready.

Sources

Kapur J, et al. Three anticonvulsants for status epilepticus (ESETT). N Engl J Med 2019;381:2103-2113 · summary: WikiJournalClub: ESETT

journal-club/jc_nice-sugar.title: JC_NICE-SUGAR
journal-club/jc_nice-sugar.content:
Journal Club: NICE-SUGAR (tight glucose control in the ICU)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Adult_Critical_Care
0. 60 second bottom line

“NICE-SUGAR (NEJM 2009) randomized 6,104 medical and surgical ICU patients to intensive glucose control (81 to 108 mg/dL) or conventional control (180 or less) with IV insulin. Ninety day death was higher with intensive control, 27.5% vs 24.9% (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.28; NNH about 38), and severe hypoglycemia was 6.8% vs 0.5%. The main limitation is no blinding. For our ICU patients, target 140 to 180 mg/dL.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators. N Engl J Med 2009;360:1283-97 ✅ ACC: NICE-SUGAR. 42 centers in Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the US; enrolled 2004 to 2008; publicly funded ✅ [1]. It answered the Leuven trials, which had suggested tight control helped surgical ICU patients.
2. PICO





























PopulationMedical and surgical ICU adults expected to stay at least 3 days ✅ [1]InterventionIV insulin to 81 to 108 mg/dL (4.5 to 6.0 mmol/L)ComparatorInsulin started above 180 mg/dL, stopped below 144, target 180 or lessOutcomeDeath from any cause at 90 daysDesignRandomized, open label, intention to treat ✅ [1]
3. Validity

Strengths: very large, multinational, patient centered outcome, publicly funded.
Red flags: not blinded (unavoidable); conventional target differed from Leuven’s control arm (180 to 215); subjective “3 days in ICU” entry criterion ✅ [1].

4. Results

































OutcomeIntensiveConventionalEffectCheck90 day death27.5%24.9%OR 1.14 (1.02 to 1.28); ARI 2.6%, NNH about 38✅✅ [1][2]Severe hypoglycemia (40 mg/dL or less)6.8%0.5%OR 14 (9.0 to 25.9)✅✅ [1][2]Subgroups (surgical vs medical, diabetes, sepsis, steroids, APACHE)No significant differences✅ [1]
5. Role in therapy
“For critically ill adults, start IV insulin above 180 mg/dL and target 140 to 180 mg/dL (ADA, AACE); tighter targets cause harm.” DKA follows its own protocol (Insulin_IV_DKA).
6. Pharmacist’s angle

Reject or modify orders targeting 80 to 110 (simulator case 38).
Watch hypoglycemia when nutrition stops but insulin keeps running.

Sources

NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators. Intensive vs conventional glucose control in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med 2009;360:1283-1297 · summary: WikiJournalClub: NICE-SUGAR
AACE: IV insulin hospital protocol (targets and NICE-SUGAR context)

journal-club/jc_ninds.title: JC_NINDS
journal-club/jc_ninds.content:
Journal Club: NINDS rt-PA Stroke Trial (alteplase within 3 hours)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Stroke_Core · Drug: Thrombolytics_Stroke
0. 60 second bottom line

“The NINDS trial (NEJM 1995) randomized 624 ischemic stroke patients within 3 hours of onset to alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) or placebo. At 3 months, more alteplase patients had minimal or no disability (Barthel 95 to 100: 50% vs 38%, NNT about 8), with no difference in death. Symptomatic brain bleeding rose from 0.6% to 6.4% (NNH 17). The main limitation is fragility and baseline imbalance. For our stroke patients, this trial is why the dose, the BP limit and the clock all matter.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study Group. N Engl J Med 1995;333(24):1581-7. PMID 7477192. The trial that led to FDA approval of alteplase for stroke. ✅✅ [1][3]
2. PICO





























PopulationIschemic stroke, treatment within 3 h of onset (half within 90 min); long bleeding exclusion list ✅ [1]InterventionAlteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% bolus, 90% over 60 min ✅✅ [2]Thrombolytics_StrokeComparatorPlaceboOutcomesPart 1: NIHSS improvement of 4 or more at 24 h. Part 2: global test of 4 scales at 3 monthsDesignTwo part, randomized, double blind, 8 US centers (624 total) ✅ [2]
3. Validity

Strengths: blinded, placebo controlled, patient centered 3 month outcomes.
Red flags: Part 1 primary was negative (47% vs 39%, not significant) ✅ [2]; baseline imbalance in stroke subtypes; fragility index about 3 ✅ [2] ⚠️ [VERIFY second source].

4. Results








































OutcomeAlteplasePlaceboEffectCheckFavorable global outcome at 3 monthsOR 1.7 (1.2 to 2.6)✅ [1]Barthel 95 to 10050%38%ARR 12%, NNT about 8✅ [2]Symptomatic ICH (36 h)6.4%0.6%NNH 17✅✅ [1][2]Death at 3 monthsNo significant difference✅✅ [1][2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Comprehensive stroke center: alteplase is still used, though AHA/ASA 2026 lists tenecteplase as equally preferred (see JC_AcT). The NINDS exclusions shaped today’s eligibility checklist.
6. Role in therapy
“For eligible ischemic stroke within the window, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) improves 3 month function at the cost of more symptomatic bleeding; tenecteplase is now an equal option.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Weigh the patient; the dose depends on it.
Waste the excess from the vial before dispensing so the full vial isn’t infused.
BP below 185/110 before, below 180/105 for 24 h after.
No antithrombotics for 24 h.

Sources

NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study Group. Tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke. N Engl J Med 1995;333:1581-1588 · summary: ClinCalc: NINDS brief summary
WikEM: NINDS
PubMed 7477192

journal-club/jc_pause.title: JC_PAUSE
journal-club/jc_pause.content:
Journal Club: PAUSE (stopping DOACs around surgery)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Anticoagulation_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“PAUSE (JAMA Internal Medicine 2019) followed 3,007 AF patients on apixaban, dabigatran or rivaroxaban through elective surgery using one simple hold schedule with no bridging and no levels. Thirty day major bleeding was 1.35%, 0.9% and 1.85%, and arterial clots were 0.16%, 0.6% and 0.37%, all within the safety targets. The main limitation is no control group. For our patients, hold 1 day before low bleed risk and 2 days before high bleed risk surgery (longer for dabigatran with CrCl below 50), and never bridge a DOAC.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Douketis JD, et al. JAMA Intern Med 2019;179(11):1469-1478 ✅ [1]. A management cohort, not a randomized trial. 23 sites, enrolled 2014 to 2018.
2. The schedule (memorize this)





























DrugLow bleed risk surgeryHigh bleed risk surgeryResumeApixaban, rivaroxaban (any kidney function); dabigatran with CrCl 50 or moreSkip the day before and the day ofSkip 2 days before, 1 day before and the day ofAbout 24 h (low) or 48 to 72 h (high) afterDabigatran with CrCl below 50Skip 2 days before, 1 day before and the day ofSkip 4, 3, 2 and 1 days before and the day ofSameNo heparin bridging; prophylactic heparin allowed after surgery for high VTE risk before the DOAC restarts ✅✅ [1][2].
3. Validity

Strengths: large, prospective, real surgeries, standardized protocol, residual drug levels measured.
Red flags: no control group; 96% white; 30 day follow up; excluded CrCl below 25 (apixaban) or below 30 (dabigatran, rivaroxaban) ✅ [1].

4. Results (30 days)








































OutcomeApixaban (1,257)Dabigatran (668)Rivaroxaban (1,082)CheckMajor bleeding1.35%0.9%1.85%✅✅ [1][2]Major bleeding, high bleed risk surgery2.96%0.88%2.95%✅ [1]Arterial thromboembolism0.16%0.6%0.37%✅ [1]Residual level below 50 ng/mL at surgery90.5%95.1%96.8%✅ [1]
5. Applicability and role in therapy
CHEST 2022 adopted this approach. “For AF patients on a DOAC having elective surgery, use the PAUSE schedule without bridging or preoperative levels.”
6. Pharmacist’s angle

Calculate CrCl for dabigatran; it changes the schedule.
Epidurals need longer holds (ASRA: 72 h for apixaban and rivaroxaban) than PAUSE (Anticoagulation_Core section 4).
Practice: Cases_Anticoag_and_Verification case 1; simulator case 17.

Sources

Douketis JD, et al. Perioperative management of AF patients on a DOAC (PAUSE). JAMA Intern Med 2019;179:1469-1478 · summary: WikiJournalClub: PAUSE

journal-club/jc_tenecteplase_followups.title: JC_Tenecteplase_Followups
journal-club/jc_tenecteplase_followups.content:
Journal Club: Tenecteplase after AcT (TRACE-2, ORIGINAL, ATTEST-2)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · First trial: JC_AcT · Drug: Thrombolytics_Stroke · Module: Stroke_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“Three more randomized, open label trials after AcT compared tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours. TRACE-2 (Lancet 2023, China, 1,430 patients), ORIGINAL (JAMA 2024, China, 1,465) and ATTEST-2 (Lancet Neurology 2024, UK, 1,858) all showed tenecteplase was noninferior for 90 day function, with the same symptomatic bleeding (1 to 2%). None showed superiority. Together with AcT, this is why AHA/ASA 2026 lists tenecteplase as equally preferred.”

1. The three trials side by side



























































TRACE-2ORIGINALATTEST-2CitationWang Y, et al. Lancet 2023Meng X, et al. JAMA 2024Muir KW, et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23(11):1087-1096Setting, N53 sites in China; 1,430China; 1,465UK; 1,858 randomized (1,777 analyzed)Primary outcomemRS 0 to 1 at 90 daysmRS 0 to 1 at 90 daysWhole mRS distribution at 90 days (ordinal)Tenecteplase vs alteplase62% vs 58%; RR 1.07 (0.98 to 1.16)72.7% vs 70.3%; RR 1.03 (0.97 to 1.09)OR 1.07 (0.90 to 1.27)Noninferior?Yes (margin RR 0.937)Yes (p 0.003)Yes (margin OR 0.75)Symptomatic ICH2% vs 2%1.2% vs 1.2%2% vs 2%90 day death7% vs 5% (not significant)4.6% vs 5.8%8% vs 8%Check✅✅ [1][2]✅ [3]✅ [4] (abstract)
2. Validity across the set

Strengths: four large trials on three continents agree; blinded outcome assessment in most ⚠️ [VERIFY each].
Red flags: all open label; noninferiority margins differ; two trials in one country; none tested tenecteplase in wake up or extended window stroke.

3. Role in therapy
“For eligible ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is equally effective and as safe as alteplase, and it’s simpler (one bolus).“
4. Pharmacist’s angle

Every trial used the stroke dose. The STEMI weight band dose (up to 50 mg) is the error to catch (simulator case 7).
One bolus means no infusion to run out or be stopped early during transfer.

Sources

Wang Y, et al. Tenecteplase vs alteplase (TRACE-2). Lancet 2023;401:645-654 · summary: ACC: TRACE-2 summary

journal-club/jc_woman.title: JC_WOMAN
journal-club/jc_woman.content:
Journal Club: WOMAN (TXA in postpartum hemorrhage)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: LD_Obstetrics_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“WOMAN (Lancet 2017) randomized about 20,000 women with postpartum hemorrhage to tranexamic acid 1 g IV (second 1 g if bleeding continued after 30 minutes) or placebo. The primary outcome, death or hysterectomy, did not differ (5.3% vs 5.5%). Death due to bleeding was lower, 1.5% vs 1.9% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.00; NNT about 250), and the benefit was concentrated in women treated within 3 hours. The main limitation is a negative primary outcome and a fragile secondary result. For our L&D patients, TXA is an add on to uterotonics, given early.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Lancet 2017;389(10084):2105-2116 ✅ Fiocruz portal: WOMAN citation. Partly funded by Pfizer, which makes TXA ✅ [1].
2. PICO





























PopulationWomen 16 or older with clinically diagnosed PPH (over 500 mL vaginal, over 1,000 mL cesarean, or instability) when the clinician was uncertain about TXA ✅ [1]InterventionTXA 1 g IV slowly (about 1 mL/min of 100 mg/mL); second 1 g if bleeding continued after 30 min or restarted within 24 h ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorPlaceboOutcomesPrimary: death from any cause or hysterectomy within 42 days. Secondary: death due to bleedingDesignDouble blind, placebo controlled, 21 countries, 193 hospitals ✅ Fiocruz portal: WOMAN citation
3. Validity

Strengths: large, blinded, placebo controlled.
Red flags: subjective inclusion (estimated blood loss, undefined instability); sample size changed during the trial; fragility index of 0 for death due to bleeding; the discussion led with a secondary outcome ✅ [1].

4. Results















































OutcomeTXAPlaceboEffectCheckDeath or hysterectomy (primary)5.3%5.5%RR 0.97 (0.87 to 1.09), not significant✅ [1]Death due to bleeding1.5%1.9%RR 0.81 (0.65 to 1.00); NNT about 250 to 274✅✅ [1][2]Death due to bleeding, treated within 3 hRR 0.69 (0.52 to 0.91)✅ [1]; NNT 100 for 1 to 3 h ✅ [2]; arm percentages ⚠️ [VERIFY]Hysterectomy3.6%3.5%No difference✅ [1]Thromboembolic eventsNo difference✅ [1]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Most deaths in WOMAN occurred in low resource settings, so the absolute benefit here is smaller. ACOG supports considering TXA when initial therapy fails. The time limit is the practical point: within 3 hours of birth.
6. Role in therapy
“For postpartum hemorrhage, TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes, repeat once after 30 minutes if needed, is a reasonable add on to uterotonics when given within 3 hours of birth.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Slow IV: about 1 mL per minute (10 minutes for 1 g).
Check time of birth before verifying.
No change to the uterotonic sequence: oxytocin first; no methylergonovine with hypertension; no carboprost with asthma.

Sources

AAFP POEM: WOMAN trial

journal-club/journal_club_template.title: Journal_Club_Template
journal-club/journal_club_template.content:
Journal Club Template (trial to bedside in 60 seconds)
Use this for every trial. Fill the Bottom line last but say it first. Built from the JAMA Users’ Guides to the Medical Literature (three questions: Are the results valid? What are the results? Will they help my patients?), the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 domains, the CONSORT 2025 reporting checklist (Hopewell et al., BMJ 2025;389:e081123), and standard pharmacy residency journal club evaluation forms.

0. The 60 second bottom line (say this first)

“[Trial name] ([journal, year]) randomized [N] [population] to [intervention] vs [comparator] for [duration]. The primary outcome, [outcome], occurred in [x%] vs [y%] (ARR [z%], NNT [n]; HR [ ], 95% CI [ ]). The main limitation is [one]. For our patients at St. Mary’s, this means [practice implication].“

1. Citation and context

Citation, trial name, funding source, authors’ conflicts of interest.
Why was this trial done? What was standard care before? What gap does it fill?
Registered (ClinicalTrials.gov number)? Was the primary outcome the same as registered?

2. PICO





























PopulationKey inclusion and exclusion criteria; who was left out (pregnant, renal impairment, elderly, peds)InterventionDrug, dose, route, duration, titrationComparatorPlacebo or active? Was the comparator dosed fairly (standard of care, right dose)?OutcomesPrimary; key secondary; safetyDesignRCT, superiority vs noninferiority vs equivalence, blinding, sites, duration
3. Are the results valid? (internal validity)

































































QuestionWhat to look forRed flagRandomized properly?Method (computer, central)Alternating days, chart numbersAllocation concealed?Central or sealed opaque envelopesInvestigators could predict the next assignmentGroups similar at baseline?Table 1Big differences in severity or key risk factorsBlinded?Patients, clinicians, outcome assessorsOpen label with a subjective outcomeAnalyzed as randomized?Intention to treat (ITT) for superiorityOnly per protocol, or a “modified ITT” that drops many patientsFollow up complete?Loss to follow up and whyLosses larger than the number of events, or unequal between groupsStopped early for benefit?Planned interim analysesEarly stopping inflates effect sizePowered?Sample size calculation and assumed event rateEvent rate much lower than assumed: underpoweredPrimary outcome meaningful?Patient oriented (death, stroke, MI) vs surrogate (A1c, LDL, INR)Surrogate only; composite driven by its softest partNoninferiority trial?Margin stated and justified; both ITT and per protocol analyzedWide margin; only ITT reported (ITT biases toward noninferiority)Multiple comparisons?Prespecified secondaries and subgroupsMany subgroups, positive one highlighted
4. What are the results?

Primary outcome: events in each arm, effect size, 95% CI, p value.
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate minus treatment event rate.
Relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR ÷ control event rate.
NNT = 1 ÷ ARR (round up). NNH = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase for harm.
Hazard ratio / odds ratio / relative risk: below 1 favors treatment (for bad outcomes). If the 95% CI crosses 1, it is not statistically significant.
Statistical vs clinical significance: a significant p value with a tiny ARR may not change practice.
Fragility index (optional): how many patients would need a different outcome to lose significance. A small number means a fragile result.
Secondary outcomes are hypothesis generating if the primary is negative.
Safety: serious adverse events, discontinuations, deaths; who paid for the safety monitoring.

5. Will it help my patients? (external validity)

Would my patient have been enrolled? (age, kidney function, comorbidities, pregnancy, weight)
Is the comparator what we use at St. Mary’s?
Is the dose, monitoring or setting realistic here? (labs, pumps, nursing time)
Formulary, cost, availability, shortages.
What do current guidelines say, and does this trial change them?

6. Strengths and limitations (pick the top 3 of each)
7. Author’s conclusion vs your conclusion

Do the data support the authors’ wording?
Your role in therapy statement: “For [patient type], [drug] is a reasonable [first line / alternative / not recommended] because [reason].”
What further research is needed?

8. Pharmacist’s angle (always add)

Dosing, renal and hepatic adjustment, interactions, monitoring, administration.
Formulary or protocol change this could support at St. Mary’s.


Formula card

































ARRCER − EERRRRARR ÷ CERNNT1 ÷ ARRRelative riskEER ÷ CER95% CI of a ratio crossing 1Not significant95% CI of a difference crossing 0Not significant
CER = control event rate; EER = experimental event rate.
How you’ll be scored (residency style)

Accurate summary of design, methods and results.
Critique: strengths, weaknesses and their impact on the result.
Conclusion with a role in therapy and limitations.
Background knowledge: disease state and the drug’s pharmacology.
Delivery: on time, clear, answers questions.

st-marys/what_leadership_values.title: What_Leadership_Values
st-marys/what_leadership_values.content:
What Leadership Values (and how to show it)
A pharmacist hired without residency training is often judged on three questions: Is she trained? Does she know the guidelines? Can she work alone? Answer each with evidence, not words.



































The questionWhat a resident would showWhat you will do”No residency”Structured training across rotationsThis 12 week plan, finished and documented. Keep log.md current; it is your training record.”Will she know the guidelines?”Quotes the guideline, year and recommendationEvery module page has the source and year. Drill the “quote it” lines.”Can she work alone on nights?”Safe, independent verification; knows when to escalateCodes, trauma and stroke modules come early. Know who to call for each service.”Will she fit in?”Easy to work with, reliable, asks good questionsTake hard shifts, close the loop on every call, thank the techs.”Will she stay current?”CE, journal club, safety alertsISMP and FDA weekly; one CE event per quarter.
What hospital pharmacy leaders are measured on

Medication errors and adverse drug events (and catching them before they reach the patient).
Turnaround time for STAT and first doses.
Joint Commission readiness: high alert drug processes, look alike sound alike, compounding compliance.
Drug cost and waste; drug shortages.
Antimicrobial stewardship metrics.

When you say something in a huddle or a call, tie it to one of these.
Relationships

After your first weeks, show the pharmacy leaders one module and one case you worked through. Ask one specific question, not a general one.
A short note at 30 and 90 days on what you completed (modules, interventions, inservice) shows the residency equivalent in writing.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Who covers NICU and PICU verification on nights?
Is there a pediatric or neonatal clinical pharmacist, and when are they on?
Where are the order sets, protocols and policies kept (intranet, Lexicomp, Cerner)?
